Chun Ri felt as though every principle of female virtue she had spent years absorbing had been overturned in a single afternoon. She and Qiuyue were now behaving like two old procuresses forcing an unwilling man, while their mistress played the role of a strong-armed merchant who bought what she pleased with no concern for anyone's consent. The two of them were presently doing their best to persuade the innocent Shen Shizhuo.

She had imagined countless versions of what life with this mistress might look like. She had never imagined it would be quite this colorful.

She stood frozen in the doorway for a moment, then managed, stiffly: "The hour is nearly upon us. The mistress is surely growing impatient. This... this young master, please — this way."

Those words alone were enough to make Shen Shizhuo's ears go red again.

He turned sharply on his heel and walked out of the room, under the gaze of both maidservants.

From his room, one had to pass through a stretch of fog forest, walking down a very dark path, before reaching Bai Qingli's room. But tonight the trees along that path had all been fitted with lanterns, and their warm orange light illuminated the whole way. He looked ahead and could see Bai Qingli's room in the distance.

As Shen Shizhuo walked toward it, he felt as though he were walking down a path lined with red carpet, and something in his chest began to burn bright and warm.

He felt as though his heart were being pulled in two directions at once — one side melting into sweet water; if he drew near, his whole self would dissolve into something soft and yielding. The other side was still struggling, repeating those admonitions over and over to himself.

He was not one of those degraded kept men from the pleasure houses. Even if she had redeemed him, he ought to preserve his own integrity. He should not yield.

But tonight the moonlight was too lovely, the candlelight too warm. When he looked toward that room, the trembling in his heart was simply impossible to suppress.

Bai Qingli's face kept rising before him — cool and composed, looking back at him from beneath the moonlight — and he felt as though the wind had gathered beneath his feet. For the first time, this path seemed so short to him. Short enough that by the time he reached the doorway, he still hadn't decided whether or not he should go in.

There was no sound from inside. He stood alone at the door for the length of time it takes to drink a cup of tea, and then, at last, he slowly pushed it open.

He would only go in to say a few words to Bai Qingli — to tell her he could not do this; that even if she truly cared for him, they would have to first make their feelings known, exchange family introductions, and go through proper courtship before anything else.

Decision made, Shen Shizhuo stepped across the threshold.

The room he entered was not large — just a table and a bed, the latter hung with a clean dark-blue rough cotton curtain. Bai Qingli lay on the low sleeping platform, eyes closed, breathing softly.

The ethereally beautiful woman lay curled like a lotus blossom on the bed, her dark hair spread across the pillow like a sweep of dark silk. Her dress and hairpins were all in place — she had clearly fallen asleep while waiting.

A breath of relief passed through Shen Shizhuo — and then, strangely, a faint, inexplicable pang of disappointment. He stood at the threshold for a moment, then finally, slowly, closed the door of the room.

The moment the door closed, only the two of them remained inside. With Bai Qingli asleep, he was, in a sense, alone — and the longing he had kept buried deepest within himself began to bubble up like water coming to a boil, rising in small bursts. He stood at the doorway watching Bai Qingli, and felt as though he were looking at the moon.

And tonight, the moon was within reach.

When Shen Shizhuo came back to himself, he had already lowered himself to one knee on the low step before the sleeping platform. One hand hovered gently beneath the fingers Bai Qingli had let fall over the edge of the bed.

Bai Qingli's fingers were slender, the tips trimmed to a neat, rounded arc, smooth and faintly pink. They rested lightly in Shen Shizhuo's broad, warm palm — her fingertips touching precisely on the line of his lifeline.

Shen Shizhuo felt as though he had been seized by the living pulse of something — as though he were caught in a web of his own making, unable to move from this position, unable to leave.

A strand of Bai Qingli's hair slipped from her shoulder and slid across Shen Shizhuo's cheek, smooth as poured ink. He looked at her moonlit face — bright as the moon, clear as water — and felt something fill his chest, something warm and nameless.

He had never met a woman like Bai Qingli — one who wore her devotion for him so openly on her face, who turned away every other person's overtures without a second thought, as though, if only he asked, she would give him everything. She did not care what the world thought, nor did she care about the lowliness of his station.

He had been born lowly. For the first time in his life, he was touched by something like grace — like being looked upon with envy, like being given warmth that asked nothing in return and expected nothing back. He was simply the best in Bai Qingli's eyes.

So this was what it felt like to be someone's favorite.

Shen Shizhuo thought: no wonder people seek love, and want so desperately to be loved.

Leaning against the bedframe, he felt the last of his gentleman's restraint crumble and shatter into ten thousand sparks — silently blazing, for no one's eyes but the darkness itself, all for Bai Qingli.

A sudden longing woke in him. He wanted to be with Bai Qingli every day.

Bai Qingli had dissolved her marriage for his sake. Did he not even have the courage to take one step forward? He was a man — how could he let a woman blaze the trail through thorns and wild brush on his behalf?

He ought to be the one walking ahead of her.

Shen Shizhuo's chest surged with feeling. He closed his palm around her fingers, but did not dare press too tightly, afraid to wake her — only held them, light as a breath.

The gentleness of his grip was like a passing breeze. But the weight of the vow he had just made within himself was like a thousand mountains.

He would sit the imperial examinations next February — just over four months away. When he passed, he would ask Bai Qingli to marry him.

Bai Qingli had taken him out of that establishment, had not despised his low station, had treated him with respect and courtesy. For a woman this good, he would offer the position of his first and only wife — a life together, two hearts devoted, one to one.

Shen Shizhuo lowered his face and pressed his forehead gently to her fingers, like an affectionate little dog seeking favor, and then settled quietly beside her on the edge of the bed, savoring this rare and precious moment.

Beyond the window, the moonlight grew softer still. Inside the room, the candlelight burned on through the night.

* * *

The following morning, when Bai Qingli woke, the room was empty. She rubbed her neck, which ached a little, and only then remembered that she had been waiting for Shen Shizhuo in the room last night — but she'd waited and waited, and no one came. Exhausted, she had fallen asleep leaning against the bed.

She still wasn't sure whether Shen Shizhuo had come at all during the night.

She rose from the sleeping platform and looked out the window at the fog forest. It was a fine autumn day — crisp air, a clear sky, thick white clouds layered at the edge of the horizon, and a slightly cool morning breeze drifting in through the window, lifting the ends of Bai Qingli's hair.

She sat lazily on the platform for a while before slowly getting to her feet.

From the moment of her rebirth until yesterday, she had been wound tightly as a spring, every step taken on the edge of a blade. One misstep and she would have ended up pierced through, just as in her previous life. But now that she had the letter of dismissal in hand and had left the Qin estate, that pressing sense of urgency had finally, mercifully, dissolved. She breathed in a rare stillness and peace.

"Qiuyue." Bai Qingli got up and went to the table to sit down. She had meant to call Qiuyue in to pour her a cup of tea — but the moment Qiuyue came through the door, her first words were: "Mistress, would you like a bath?"

Bai Qingli reconsidered. She did still have to go to the Bai family today — another difficult fight ahead. She nodded in agreement. She had wanted to add, "and heat a pot of water for tea while you're at it," but Qiuyue had already shot out the door like a gust of wind before she could say another word.

Qiuyue ran straight to the kitchen at the back, where Chun Ri had already been waiting at the kitchen door to gossip.

"The mistress wants a bath, the mistress wants a bath!" Qiuyue pumped her fist, her face flushing bright red. "I knew it — that male fox-spirit really has some skill! He kept the mistress occupied until just now before she woke up!"

The fox-spirit had entered at dusk the evening before and hadn't emerged from the room until morning. When Qiuyue had asked him "how well did you serve her," the man had muttered something unintelligible and slipped away. And now the mistress was still sleeping when the sun was already high in the sky!

He had been so coy and bashful last night — ears practically on fire — and yet here he was, apparently quite the handful once he finally got started. These kept men from the pleasure houses really did know how to hide what they were capable of!

"That rascal, looking like someone who'd never so much as sniffed a spice jar, ears burning so red last night — I thought he was just easily flustered! Turns out once he's in the bed he won't get out!"

Her words took on a faintly sour note. She had the nagging feeling that ever since this kept man arrived, the mistress didn't dote on her as much as before — all day long, it was just Anu this, Anu that.

Qiuyue was almost furious at herself for not being a man.

If she were a man, she'd have claimed the first place on the mistress's bed herself. What business would this fox-spirit have there!

Chun Ri kept her head down and fed the stove, not joining in — but in her heart, she was doing a little yearning of her own.

A fox-spirit that handsome? Who wouldn't want one? Obedient and well-mannered, with a scholarly air — when he stood quietly, he was like a white crane beneath the pines, all elegance and bearing.

She used to think a woman was supposed to serve her husband, follow the Three Obediences and Four Virtues, and that was how you made your way through life. But looking at the mistress now — with a generous dowry in her possession, loyal maidservants at her side, and a kept man waiting to attend her — was this life not freer than anything the Qin estate had to offer?

She had always been the sort of girl who dared to want and dared to act. On the spot, she grabbed a handful of kindling and shoved it hard into the stove, then made a silent, solemn vow.

She was going to save up her money — and go buy herself an obedient kept man to wait on her!

Save money. Buy a man.

* * *

After her bath, Bai Qingli changed into a pale sky-blue crossed-collar gauze silk dress, wearing only a simple silver hairpin, and left Fog Forest Courtyard with Qiuyue driving the carriage toward the Bai family estate.

As Bai Qingli's carriage pulled away from Fog Forest Courtyard, she did not notice that a figure was crouched in the branches of a distant tree just outside the courtyard gate, watching her carriage with burning eyes. When the carriage had gone far enough, those eyes shifted back to the courtyard itself.

Once certain Bai Qingli was not coming back, the figure dropped from the tree and slipped soundlessly over the wall into Fog Forest Courtyard.

At that point, the only people remaining in Fog Forest Courtyard besides Shen Shizhuo were Chun Ri, who was in the storeroom taking stock of the mistress's dowry piece by piece and recording everything in a ledger so it could be located when needed, and Shen Shizhuo himself, who was in the study reading.

He was working through a volume on statecraft — a treatise on the principles of governance. He had studied such texts before; though his childhood had been solitary, he had not lacked for books, and someone had also been engaged to teach him martial arts. Unfortunately—

"Who's there?" After barely two pages, Shen Shizhuo shot to his feet and turned toward the door of the study.

He had heard light, deliberate footsteps and the sound of breathing carefully suppressed. It could not possibly be Chun Ri.

chapters.title: Twenty eight
chapters.content:
The person outside the study seemed not to have anticipated being discovered so easily. He hesitated outside for a long moment, then stepped out from among the fog trees into the open.

He was a composed man in his forties, with the unmistakable air of someone forged on the battlefield — decisive and ruthless. A scar ran across his forehead. He was dressed in rough short-cut clothing, his face uncovered. The front of his chest and the back of his waist bulged slightly, suggesting concealed blades.

Through the wooden window of the study, Shen Shizhuo and the stranger appraised each other's threat in the same instant.

Shen Shizhuo had a lean frame, carrying the particular slenderness of a young man still growing into himself, though he stood tall. He did not flinch at the sight of the intruder. He remained standing quietly behind the writing desk and asked in a clear, calm voice: "Were you sent by the mistress to kill me?"

The man's movement stalled.

He stared at the composed expression on Shen Shizhuo's face — Shen Shizhuo looked as though he already knew everything — and for a moment the man didn't know how to respond. He thought for a beat, then clasped his hands in a respectful bow and said: "Young Master, this subordinate was sent by the Master to find you. The Master wishes to bring you home. As for the mistress's affairs — this subordinate knows nothing of that."

Shen Shizhuo's lips pressed slowly together.

Without thinking, he looked around the room.

The narrow study, the writing desk with its faint smell of old wood, the rough brushes and ink and paper — nothing approaching the quality he had known as a child. But he liked it here.

He had no desire to go back.

Shen Shizhuo had known from a young age that he was different from other children.

From birth, he had lived in a remote mountain temple. There was no one there but a wet nurse, a maidservant, and a study companion. Each day a tutor came to teach him the classics of governing a household, ruling a state, bringing peace to the world. As he grew older, he was also taught martial arts.

His life was materially comfortable. There was always fish and meat on the table. The wet nurse who cared for him wore gold and silver. And yet — all other children had parents. He did not.

He had once snuck out of the temple in the dead of night to watch how other families lived, and gradually, from those observations, he had pieced together a theory.

He suspected he was the illegitimate son of someone from a powerful household. Perhaps a man of great standing had fathered him with a woman of low birth, and not wanting to discard him entirely, yet unable to raise him openly, had found a remote place, arranged for teachers, and waited. Waited until he was accomplished enough. Waited until he had grown. Then his father and mother would come to claim him.

They never came.

Instead, a group of masked men arrived — about ten of them — and surrounded the ancient temple. They cut down the wet nurse, the maidservant, and the study companion. Having trained in martial arts since childhood, Shen Shizhuo fought his way out through sheer desperation, following a mountain stream downhill until he reached the capital. Found half-dead by a procurer from the pleasure house, he had been taken in and made into a kept man.

Shen Shizhuo could more or less guess why someone had tried to kill him. His existence had been discovered by his father's primary wife, and she had decided to eliminate him entirely.

Anyone who could track him down at such a time was either sent by his father or by his father's wife. His father's men would protect him. His father's wife's men would only want him dead.

He had no intention of getting entangled in any of it.

"Go back and tell him that everything about him has nothing to do with me." He said: "I will change my name. I will not return."

The man's cheek twitched slightly. He clearly hadn't expected such a direct refusal. He had a head full of arguments ready to make, but in the end could only squeeze out one dry sentence: "Young Master, the Master had his difficulties back then. Since learning of your existence, the Master has been unable to eat or sleep."

Shen Shizhuo remained unmoved.

The man added: "Boundless wealth and fortune lies just within reach. Young Master — take one look before deciding whether you want it or not." Shen Shizhuo shook his head coldly.

The man stood there for a moment, then finally gritted his teeth and said: "Should the Young Master change his mind, simply place a red lantern at the gate, and this subordinate will come." With that, he turned and left.

Shen Shizhuo watched the man's retreating figure with cold eyes until he had disappeared entirely, then turned back to his desk and resumed reading.

He had grown up alone and withdrawn; he had no longing for family. And through the attack at the old temple, he could well imagine what kind of murky and treacherous place his birth father inhabited. He wanted no part of any of it. He only wanted to live quietly in Fog Forest Courtyard — reading, studying, passing the examinations.

And asking for her hand.

* * *

The unexpected visitor to Fog Forest Courtyard came and went, known to no one but Shen Shizhuo. Meanwhile, Bai Qingli had arrived at the Bai family estate.

The Bai household had been beset by misfortune of late.

First there had been the whole affair with Bai Yunhe, and then Bai Qingli's father had made an enemy in the bureaucratic world, stumbled badly, and in his bitterness had taken to frequenting brothels and wine houses, not returning home for a full day and night. Bills from such establishments kept arriving one after another; Bai Madam's chest was so tight with suppressed resentment she could barely breathe, but she had nowhere to vent it.

Bai Yunhe lived in constant dread that the whole business would come to light. He had been making errors at court and had already been sharply rebuked twice by the Minister of Justice — his future father-in-law — and now walked as though treading on thin ice every single day. The only one in the household who remained entirely ignorant of what had happened was the legitimate daughter, Bai Yunstrost.

She had also been present when the Bai family attended the banquet at the Qin estate, but this girl was only fourteen this year and was still in the midst of marriage negotiations. She was a naturally guileless and romantic soul who had no idea of the treacherous undercurrents running between the Qin and Bai families. She had taken no part in harming Bai Qingli in her previous life, and bore her no ill will. True to the principle of leaving in peace those who do not seek conflict, Bai Qingli had spared her. When Bai Yunstrost attended the Qin banquet, Bai Qingli had arranged a separate flower pavilion just for her, inviting her to bring some close friends to enjoy themselves there, keeping her well away from all the unpleasantness.

To be invited to the General's estate and have an entire pavilion arranged exclusively for her — Bai Yunstrost took it as a special honor and a mark of affection from her elder sister, and felt enormously gratified. She brought several of her closest companions and spent the whole time enjoying herself from beginning to end. On the way out, Chun Ri personally escorted her home, and she heard not a single unsavory word about what had occurred. To this day she still had no idea that her elder brother had been the victim of someone else's scheme.

So when Bai Qingli arrived, Bai Yunstrost was actually quite looking forward to seeing her — but the gatekeeper only gave notice of the visit, and before she could even catch a glimpse of Bai Qingli, Bai Madam had shooed her back to her own room and forbidden her to come out.

When Bai Qingli reached Bai Madam's courtyard, Bai Madam was already waiting at the entrance.

Despite her private troubles, Bai Madam's appearance was immaculate. She wore a crimson crossed-collar pleated skirt with mercury-silver wave patterns stitched along the hem, her hair pinned with a full set of pure silver accessories dyed indigo. At first glance, she looked dignified and graceful.

As Bai Qingli entered, Bai Madam dismissed every maidservant. Only then did she take Bai Qingli by the hand and sit her down — without even pausing to pour tea — and immediately demanded: "What is being planned at the General's estate?"

Bai Madam still did not know that Bai Qingli had been dismissed. Bai Qingli had slipped away from the Qin household without a sound, and the Qin family, knowing the whole affair was shameful from start to finish, had made no effort to publicize it.

By convention, if Qin Shanyue wished to formally dismiss Bai Qingli, he would have had to summon the Bai family and lay out all the details openly. The standard process for such a dismissal also involved both parties offering formal apologies to preserve each other's reputations. But the confrontation between Qin Shanyue and Bai Qingli the day before had escalated beyond recovery, compounded by the whole entanglement involving Bai Yunhe and Zhao Hongzhu — and neither Qin Shanyue nor the Bai family knew how to face each other. So no formal meeting had been called.

Qin Shanyue's posture made it clear that he intended for the two households to have no further dealings with each other: he would take Zhao Hongzhu, and hold no grudge against Bai Yunhe; he had dismissed Bai Qingli, and wanted no trouble from the Bai family in return. One offense balanced by another, and they would be quits.

If Bai Qingli simply explained everything to Bai Madam, Bai Madam would of her own accord call for a retreat — close her eyes and cover her ears and pretend she had heard nothing. If Bai Madam went to the Qin estate now, the Qin family would assume she was there to discuss the dismissal and attempt some form of negotiation, since a woman being dismissed was deeply humiliating and the Qin family was not an enemy one could afford to make. Even if the marriage could not be salvaged, creating enmity served no one's interests; better to reach a quiet resolution where possible.

In reality, Bai Madam still had no idea Bai Qingli had been dismissed. Who could have guessed that Bai Qingli would cover everything up so completely — refusing to return home even after the dismissal? To avoid being noticed by the Bai household's own maidservants and nurses, she had not even gone to her own estates, going directly to hide in Fog Forest Courtyard instead.

What Bai Qingli was exploiting was the shared instinct of both families: neither wanted the scandal broadcast. Neither wanted to speak of it. In the space between their mutual silence, she had room to maneuver.

"The General's estate is planning to have Zhao Hongzhu married into the Bai family."

Bai Qingli lowered her eyes and gave Bai Madam the first piece of news — one devastating enough to shatter her composure.

"Impossible!"

Bai Madam's voice landed hard as a blow: "Our Bai family would never take in such a woman!"

Bai Qingli said nothing. She leaned back in her chair, raised one slender hand to lift the nearby teapot, and poured herself a cup. The finest green tea from south of the Yangtze — one sip, and the fragrance was rich and mellow. Only a little cool.

To properly appreciate tea, the water must be brought to a full, rolling boil. Just as with the affairs of this world — what is tepid and unhurried can never yield the full, lingering depth of the thing. The fire burning now was still too low. Bai Qingli didn't mind tipping in a little more oil.

"Qingli, you know our Bai family's standards. When you were young you weren't even allowed to go out on the street unchaperoned. You were raised on the Four Arts — a true daughter of a great house. How could someone like Zhao Hongzhu ever enter our family? I absolutely refuse!"

Bai Madam was so furious that her manner of speaking to Bai Qingli had taken on a rebuking tone. Bai Qingli nodded, cradling her cup, and said: "Mother, I feel the same way. I told the Qin household as much — and I had quite a fierce argument with the General over it. As things stand now, the General has placed me under house restrictions. He is convinced that Bai Yunhe, in a drunken state, took advantage of Zhao Hongzhu, and he has made up his mind that the Bai family must offer Zhao Hongzhu some kind of redress. He also said that if the Bai family refuses, he will not only bring charges against Bai Yunhe — he will also dismiss me. Hearing all this, I was so distressed that I came home to find you."

The words struck Bai Madam like a thunderclap. In a fit of fury she swept the teapot off the table — it hit the floor with a crack — and shot to her feet, breaking into a torrent of cursing.

"Outrageous! Outrageous! I have never seen anyone conduct themselves so unconscionably! Has the years of fighting at the frontier addled Qin Shanyue's brain? It is clearly Zhao Hongzhu who schemed against our Yunhe! And he can still speak such utter nonsense? He has completely lost all sense of law and decency — he thinks our Bai family has no one to stand up for us!"

Bai Madam's chest heaved violently. Both her eyes had gone red with fury. She had been an official's wife for decades and had never encountered such coercion in marriage matters. If Zhao Hongzhu were a respectable young woman raised like a daughter by the Qin Old Madam, she would have held her nose and accepted it — granting her the status of a secondary wife wouldn't even be beneath Zhao Hongzhu's dignity. But Zhao Hongzhu had an ambiguous relationship with Qin Shanyue himself, and then had somehow ended up in bed with her son under murky circumstances — how could she ever allow a woman like that through her door?

"Mother, I believe there may still be room to turn this around,"

Bai Madam was shaking with rage, her handkerchief nearly wrung apart in her hands. Then Bai Qingli, of all people, spoke up in a conciliatory tone: "All of this is Qin Shanyue's doing, but the Old Madam is a sensible woman. Perhaps you could go speak with her and have her talk some reason into Qin Shanyue."

At the mention of the Old Madam, Bai Qingli also sighed. A look of weary resignation crossed her usually composed face: "All these years in the Qin household, I have attended on my mother-in-law every day. The Old Madam naturally has affection for me in her heart. When she heard about Zhao Hongzhu's scandalous behavior, she was so distressed she fell ill. Mother, if the General truly can't be reasoned with, just let it go — go speak gently with the Old Madam instead. She might just be the one who can still turn things around."

Some of the blazing fury in Bai Madam settled. She sat back down, thinking Bai Qingli had a point.

The affairs of this world are tangled like threads within threads — pull one strand and the whole web trembles. Most people can only struggle within the net, searching for some way through. A few have the force to cut their way out with a blade — but most have neither the ability to break free nor the constitution to bear the consequences. So they endure, calculating every step forward and back, and even when they swallow down something that breaks their teeth, they must smile and pretend it never happened.

What of it, that it's sickening? What of it, that it's wretched? They all live in the same city. Even sworn enemies have to manage a surface of civility, so as not to become a laughingstock for all to see.

"You're right." Bai Madam smoothed the creases that had appeared in her sleeve. Her gold ring with its jade-green stone slid over the crimson silk cuff, the fabric smooth and yielding beneath it. She gentled her tone slightly and repeated: "You're right."

After a brief pause, she added: "Life must go on. This is just one obstacle to get past. Qingli, you rest here for now. I'll send a calling card today and pay a visit to the Old Madam tomorrow."

"Mother, this is a matter that cannot wait," Bai Qingli said, shaking her head. "Never mind the formalities. Go directly to find the Old Madam now. If we delay even a little, things may take a turn for the worse."

Bai Madam was already fretting and unsettled. At Bai Qingli's prompting, she felt as though a flame had been lit beneath her chair — she simply could not sit still. After a few hasty words with Bai Qingli, she rose immediately and called for the carriage to take her to Qilin Street and pay her call on the Qin Old Madam.

"Mother — if you happen to see Zhao Hongzhu, do not engage with her. That woman bears no goodwill toward our family. Don't say a single word to her. Go directly to the Old Madam."

Bai Qingli gave her careful instructions: "And Mother, be sure to remember — when you see the Old Madam, speak to her gently and kindly. The Old Madam understands what is what in her heart. She inclines toward our Bai family's side. Say exactly what is on your mind, clearly and plainly: tell her that our Bai family cannot possibly accept Zhao Hongzhu into our household, and that our brother's promising future absolutely cannot be ruined by Zhao Hongzhu's hand."

Bai Madam composed herself, replied with a simple "Don't worry, I know what I'm doing," then gathered her skirts and boarded the carriage.

The wheels turned, the sound of hoofbeats faded down the street, and once the carriage had completely disappeared around the corner, Bai Qingli turned and walked back to her own carriage.

The elderly nurse at the Bai household gate assumed Bai Qingli was also returning to the Qin estate, and stood in the doorway with a bowing farewell. Bai Qingli did not spare her a glance. She turned and stepped up into the carriage.

Qiuyue drove them away.

The carriage wound through several turns and departed from the Bai estate.

* * *

Bai Madam's carriage traveled for half an hour before reaching the rear gate of the Qin estate on Qilin Street. Bai Madam sent her maidservant ahead to announce the visit, and within moments a young woman came out to receive her.

Bai Madam had not attended Bai Qingli's banquet at the Qin estate, so she had not seen Zhao Hongzhu then — but she recognized her all the same.

The dazzling Miss Zhao who had once been the talk of the capital, like a blossom not yet fully opened, had now grown into her beauty. The imperious willfulness of her younger years had softened with time, replaced by a certain radiant elegance. Her hair was pinned with gold and jade ornaments, and she wore a long bright-green dress with a matching cloak of the same color, giving her the impression of a stroke of spring itself as she moved. When she caught sight of Bai Madam, she gave a proper bow of deference.

"Hongzhu pays her respects to Madam Bai."

Zhao Hongzhu's bow was a pleasure to behold, and when she straightened, the hairpins in her hair swayed delicately. Her manners were impeccable. One cannot bring oneself to strike a smiling face — Bai Madam had to swallow all her fury, though she could not produce even the semblance of a smile: "I have business with the Old Madam."

Seeing the look on Bai Madam's face, Zhao Hongzhu showed nothing outwardly, though a flicker of private satisfaction and contempt passed through her mind.

Yesterday, Bai Qingli had left with such arrogance — as though she would never look back. Yet here she was the very next day, sending her own birth mother to front for her.

Did Bai Qingli really believe that a Bai Madam could shake Qin Shanyue's resolve?

As things stood, Bai Qingli had already been dismissed, Qin Shanyue was going to marry her, and Bai Yunhe ought to count himself lucky. The Bai family ought to have the sense to quietly keep their distance — and yet here they were at the Qin estate. Did they still think the Qin family would show Bai Qingli any mercy?

"What terrible timing — the Old Madam caught a chill a few days ago and has been unwell."

Zhao Hongzhu smiled pleasantly while speaking hollow niceties to Bai Madam, her manner respectful enough on the surface, though the satisfaction in her eyes was impossible to conceal.

At this moment, she was the one who held authority in the Qin household. A visitor who showed up without a calling card, expecting to see the mistress — she was perfectly entitled to turn such a person away.

Bai Madam's brow furrowed in immediate irritation: "Zhao Hongzhu, leave yourself some room to maneuver! Do you truly think the Bai family is so easily pushed around? Do I actually have to come here and bang on the Qin family's door with a crowd behind me before you feel a shred of alarm?"

The ferocity in Bai Madam's expression gave Zhao Hongzhu a start, and she belatedly realized that if Bai Madam were truly pushed to her breaking point, she herself stood to gain nothing from it.

"Since Madam Bai has come to call, I will announce your arrival for you." Zhao Hongzhu curved her lips into a slight smile and maintained the full appearance of propriety. In any case, Bai Qingli's dismissal was already done and settled. Even if Bai Madam had the tongue of an angel, she could not change the Qin family's minds.

Once Zhao Hongzhu gave notice, the Qin Old Madam made herself get up from her sickbed.

She had been resting and recovering these past days and had regained some of her vital energy — she was now alert and had taken in some food. When she heard a member of the Bai family had come calling, she could more or less guess the reason, and her expression immediately settled into one of cold readiness to settle scores. She dragged herself up, had her hair dressed, and was helped by attendants from her chamber to the main reception hall.

The Bai family woman had come to plead for her daughter!

Hmph. The things Bai Qingli had done — the mere thought of them curdled the Old Madam's blood with hatred.

She was going to make Bai Qingli pay dearly. She was going to thoroughly humiliate Bai Madam. The beloved nurse who had served her for so many years could not be allowed to die for nothing.

Fierce hatred propped up her aging body. By the time she reached the front hall, Bai Madam had been waiting for some time already — the tea in the cups had gone cold. It was late in the ninth month, bordering on the tenth; the wind in the capital had turned bone-chillingly cold. A warming brazier was only lit after the Old Madam took her seat — and clearly it had been lit for the Old Madam's sake, not for the guest.

The Old Madam was indeed in poor health. The pallor of illness could not be hidden from her face; the skin drooped downward in loose folds, and as she walked, her wide robes swayed with her skin, the very picture of someone whose days were numbered.

Seeing the Old Madam, Bai Madam too felt a knot of frustration pressing in her chest. Zhao Hongzhu had deliberately made her wait; not a single maidservant had been left in the front hall to pour tea or bring water. She had not been treated with such neglect in many years, and however good her composure, she could not help but let a chill creep into her expression.

"Old Madam Qin." Once the Old Madam was seated, Bai Madam eased slightly the coolness on her face. She ran the ring on her finger across her cuff once more, steadied herself, and sat up straight: "I have come today on the principle that enemies are better reconciled than held onto. We exchanged calling cards, we joined our families through marriage — why must things be pushed to such an unpleasant pass?"

What Bai Madam said could not quite be described as tactful or roundabout — she simply wasn't capable of being tactful. After speaking those words, she already felt somewhat regretful, and softened her tone slightly.

She continued: "Old Madam, I can see that you truly care for Qingli in your heart — look how she has upset you. I'll speak plainly: no matter what — even if the Emperor himself were to issue a decree — I would give my life to push it back. I could not allow Zhao Hongzhu to marry into the Bai family."

The Old Madam had been sitting there, eyes half-closed, composing herself in all her dignity, fully expecting Bai Madam to have come to apologize and plead on behalf of her ruthless and shameless daughter. But who could have anticipated that the very first thing out of Bai Madam's mouth would be: "I could not allow Zhao Hongzhu to marry into the Bai family."

The Old Madam's eyes snapped open in startled confusion. When she spoke, her voice came out thick and hoarse, as though she had a mouthful of phlegm stuck in her throat: "What did you say? Hongzhu marrying into the Bai family—"

Had she gone senile, with ears that no longer worked? Or had Bai Madam lost her mind? Hongzhu was her treasured darling — the one who was to marry her Shanyue. What did that have to do with the Bai family's legitimate son?

Bai Madam paused, then shifted to a gentler tone and continued: "Old Madam, at the banquet that day, Zhao Hongzhu also drugged my son — that is how this whole thing came about. If one were to argue it out properly, my son is the innocent party. But out of consideration for Zhao Hongzhu's reputation and dignity, our Bai family is willing to offer some form of reparation — whether monetary compensation or something else — only she absolutely cannot enter our household. A forced marriage makes for a bitter one; it would only lead to misery for all parties down the road. Better to speak plainly now rather than ruin two lives."

As Bai Madam spoke, the Old Madam looked at her steadily. The Old Madam's eyes had truly grown dim with age; everything around her had blurred and wavered at the edges. All she could see clearly was Bai Madam's carmined lips moving open and shut, saying words she could not begin to comprehend.

Then, in a single moment, the Qin Old Madam abruptly flung her dragon-headed walking cane aside. With trembling fingers gripping the wooden armrest beside her, she struggled to her feet and cried out in a high voice: "Hongzhu — Hongzhu!"

Because this was to be a discussion of family dishonor, the Old Madam had left her maidservants waiting in the outer room. Even her most trusted Stewardess Liu was dead. In the entire front hall, there were only the two of them. The dragon-headed cane clattered to the floor, and when the old woman burst out with those anguished cries, Bai Madam gave a start.

She had never seen the Old Madam like this before. She had the frail, tottering look of someone standing on the edge of the grave — and yet each cry seemed to draw blood, each one higher and more piercing than the last. The Old Madam even attempted to go down the steps, but her foot caught on nothing and her whole bent body lurched forward and crumpled — the ornaments in her white hair flew loose and clattered across the marble floor with a series of loud, scattered cracks.

Like an ominous sign, it made Bai Madam's chest heave in violent, rapid pulses. She clutched her handkerchief and rose to her feet — she had not said anything inflammatory; she had spoken with nothing but sincere, honest concern. Why was the Old Madam reacting so violently?

The sound of the Old Madam's frail body hitting the floor was alarming enough to send the blood rushing to Bai Madam's temples. At precisely that moment, a maidservant from the outer room swept in through the beaded curtain. At the sight of the Old Madam collapsed on the ground, she let out a startled scream and rushed forward to help — and that scream struck Bai Madam's chest like a fist squeezing around her heart.

Just then, Zhao Hongzhu came rushing in from the outer room as well. She had moved so fast that her green cloak billowed up behind her, carrying a gust of perfume as she flung herself down beside the Old Madam on the floor.

"Old Madam!"

Zhao Hongzhu dropped to her knees to help the Old Madam up, her smooth, slender, pink-tipped fingers clasping the Old Madam's dry, withered, age-spotted hand. She had meant to lift the Old Madam up — but the Old Madam seized her in turn, grabbing her wrist and pinning it down, pulling Zhao Hongzhu down with her.

The dark tendons beneath the Old Madam's aged brown skin stood out taut as cords. Her sunken chest wheezed like a broken bellows. Her clouded eyes were fixed on Zhao Hongzhu's face with a ferocious, drilling intensity.

Zhao Hongzhu had never seen the Old Madam look at her like that — dark and vicious, like a lioness roused to fury. Though she appeared at any moment to be about to breathe her last, the light blazing from those eyes was something Zhao Hongzhu could not bear to meet directly.

"Old Madam."

Zhao Hongzhu's voice trembled with the strain of holding herself together. She looked at the Old Madam with eyes full of concern and asked: "What happened? How did you fall? Hongzhu is here—"

This should have been a glorious day — the Old Madam raging at Bai Madam, finally venting all her accumulated fury. Why was the Old Madam looking at her like this?

"You and Bai Yunhe — what exactly is going on between you?" The Old Madam's purplish, withered lips trembled as she gripped Zhao Hongzhu's wrist, squeezing that sentence out through the gaps between her teeth.

The look of concern on Zhao Hongzhu's face froze in place. The smile cracked open at a hairline seam, revealing the cold beneath. Still locked in her half-kneeling posture before the Old Madam, she went rigid, the color draining from her radiant face little by little, her eyes filling with panic and dread.

How could the Old Madam know about this?

Zhao Hongzhu snapped her head around. Her startled, furious, and resentful gaze fell upon Bai Madam standing to one side.

The only possible answer was that Bai Madam had told the Old Madam. But why would Bai Madam do that? Qin Shanyue had already decided to marry her. The Bai family certainly had no desire to invite further trouble — everyone had been pretending not to see it, and it would have been easy enough to bury the matter quietly. Why would Bai Madam go out of her way to expose it?

The moment Bai Madam caught Zhao Hongzhu's gaze, she sensed, dimly, that something had gone wrong — though she couldn't identify what. Cold sweat was already seeping from her fingertips.

The Old Madam suddenly let out a thunderous cry, eyes blazing with a sudden fierce light like a final flare of dying embers. Somehow she found strength enough to shake off the maidservants trying to support her. They dropped to their knees all around her in panic, while the Old Madam, by sheer force of will, hauled herself upright. "What is your relationship with Bai Yunhe?"

A cry escaped Zhao Hongzhu's throat, half scream, half plea: "Old Madam!"

That wail made Bai Madam, standing nearby, feel as though every organ inside her had been shaken loose, all of it churning together in a knot. She took an involuntary step backward, the backs of her knees catching the wooden chair behind her, and she went rigid all over.

By now, even Bai Madam understood. The Qin Old Madam had known nothing — nothing at all — about Zhao Hongzhu and Bai Yunhe. By coming here, Bai Madam had unwittingly punctured a screen of shameful concealment and dragged every ugly secret into the glare of noon, letting the foul and festering matter spill out freely, in plain view of all.

"I am asking you — what is your relationship!" The Old Madam looked half-maddened now, her thin white hair hanging loose at the sides of her face. The maidservants were on their knees all around her, and Bai Madam stood watching — but the Old Madam no longer cared. She stared only at Zhao Hongzhu's face.

The Qin Old Madam had navigated the treacherous inner courts of powerful households for most of her life. She had witnessed extravagant excess, noble ladies who kept kept men, and servant girls who conducted illicit affairs with manservants. She had seen countless outrageous spectacles, and it had sharpened her eyes to a ruthless keenness. One look at Zhao Hongzhu's expression now, and the Old Madam knew beyond doubt: Bai Madam was telling the truth.

A mouthful of old blood surged to the back of her throat. The Old Madam felt as though her entire body had been turned to ice. She stared at Zhao Hongzhu's face, her voice shaking, and drove each word like a spike into the heart: "I treated you as a daughter! I treated you as a daughter!"

Zhao Hongzhu's wrist was gripped so hard the bones ached, a red mark rising where the Old Madam's fingers pressed. She choked out through her tears: "Old Madam, it wasn't like that — it was all a misunderstanding, all a misunderstanding."

The Old Madam grew only more furious. With her wild white hair, she shrieked with something close to madness: "A misunderstanding? Have you no mouth? Do you not know whose bed you ended up in? Were you incapable of speaking when someone ruined you? You kept all of it hidden — you dared not let me know — and yet you went ahead planning a wedding! You presumed to enter my Qin household with a sullied body, to marry my son? Wishful thinking — utterly wishful thinking!"

She loved Zhao Hongzhu, yes — but that love had its limits. When it came to a choice between Qin Shanyue and Zhao Hongzhu, she would, without the slightest hesitation, choose Qin Shanyue. That was why, the very moment the Zhao family had met with ruin, she had immediately begun seeking another match for Qin Shanyue.

Three years ago, she had refused to let Zhao Hongzhu — daughter of a condemned traitor — marry her son, for fear of dragging down his career. Three years later, she would equally refuse to let Zhao Hongzhu — a woman whose chastity was lost — marry her son, for fear of corrupting the sanctity of his household. When Zhao Hongzhu had bullied Bai Qingli, she had felt it perfectly natural for Bai Qingli to yield, because she favored Zhao Hongzhu. But when Zhao Hongzhu began to taint Qin Shanyue himself, her fury became impossible to contain. In the end, it came back to this: as long as a calamity didn't fall on her own head, one could be generous. But when it finally did?

At first the Old Madam had only felt disappointment — but in the end, out of nowhere, a violence rose in her. She flung Zhao Hongzhu's wrist aside and struck her hard across the face.

The jade-and-gold ring on the Old Madam's finger raked across Zhao Hongzhu's cheek, drawing a thin line of blood. Still not satisfied, the Old Madam's face twisted with fury as she screamed: "If not for you — if not for you — how would our Qin family have come to this? You are nothing but a curse, a demon who destroys everyone you touch! You should have died at the northern border — why did you have to come back and ruin us? If you hadn't returned, how would Stewardess Liu have died?"

"A woman like you — and you want to marry my son? You think you deserve to marry my son? As long as I draw breath, you will never bring disorder into my Qin family's honor!"

Every word the Old Madam spat landed on Zhao Hongzhu's face along with her fury. Just moments ago, Zhao Hongzhu had been wearing an expression of remorse — but something in what the Old Madam said cut deep, and suddenly Zhao Hongzhu snapped her head up, her swollen red face set with fury, and said each word with deliberate weight: "I will marry him. I will marry him. And he will marry me — he said he would, and so he will. What he wants — you cannot stop!"

The moon hangs at the mountain's peak, the flowering lanterns blaze on the branches — beyond reach, impossible to cup in one's hands — and yet she will have them, even so.

She would climb, step by step, through this house that devoured people. She would stand on the heads of everyone who looked down on her with their contempt and disdain. She would use her ruined life to stir up the waters. So what if she was tainted? So what if her chastity was lost? Others had things; she had them too. What others didn't have — she would have as well. Ten miles of crimson wedding gifts, a thousand lanterns lining the street — she would have her own, singular share. The more those people despised her, the better she intended to live.

She knew she could.

Because Qin Shanyue loved her.

Love — that one word — could cut through thorns, conquer the unconquerable, and hold back ten thousand soldiers.

"How dare you!" The Old Madam let out a furious bellow, seemingly about to lunge forward and strike Zhao Hongzhu again — but the moment she lifted her foot, that aged body gave way and fell straight down. She fell in the direction of where Zhao Hongzhu was standing. Zhao Hongzhu stood right there — red-eyed, face swollen — and watched the Old Madam collapse to the ground with cold indifference. Not a flicker of emotion crossed her face, not the slightest move to reach out and catch her.

The maidservants were all still kneeling. When the Old Madam fell, they scrambled to help her, to fetch a physician, to run out and call for assistance. In the chaos that followed, Zhao Hongzhu simply stood where she was, her face a blank.

A maidservant's shoulder caught Zhao Hongzhu by accident as she rushed past, and Zhao Hongzhu was knocked back half a step. The impact seemed to jolt her out of that hollow stillness — and she became suddenly aware, once more, of what was happening around her.

When that dark, hollow gaze of Zhao Hongzhu's fell on Bai Madam, Bai Madam's legs went weak. She stumbled backward and sat down heavily in the chair behind her. Cold sweat slid down Bai Madam's forehead. The flesh of her face trembled slightly, and yet she could not get out a single word.

She knew — she had caused a catastrophe.

Bai Madam was no great intellect, but she was nearly forty years old, and her mind had always been adequate enough. Having watched this whole scene unfold before her, she could, naturally, piece together what had happened.

* * *

chapters.title: Twenty nine
chapters.content:
When he stepped beneath the entrance plaque of the Qin estate, he felt a brief, disorienting vertigo.

In the past, whenever he returned to the estate from the city, a slender white-robed figure would always be waiting at the gate. Once he entered, everything would have been arranged for him. All he had to do was follow Bai Qingli back to the Lotus Courtyard, where he could shed the weight of the day and rest.

At the time, it had seemed the most ordinary thing in the world.

As his black boots crossed the threshold, the sounds of commotion inside the Qin estate reached his ears. Qin Shanyue, already exhausted, felt every nerve draw taut again. He walked into the courtyard with a furrowed brow and found several older servant women dragging Zhao Hongzhu by force. Her hair had come loose, and she was struggling and fighting back against them.

The newly made green cloak had been torn from her shoulders and trodden on the ground, leaving muddy footprints. The sight cut into Qin Shanyue's eyes.

"Stop!" Qin Shanyue's single bark of command drowned out every screaming and shouting woman in the courtyard. The servants and maidservants all dropped to their knees. Zhao Hongzhu, who had been dragged and pulled down to the ground, looked up at the sound of Qin Shanyue's voice with reddened eyes.

That look shattered something in Qin Shanyue's chest. He strode forward. With the powerful sweep of arms trained for battle, he gathered Zhao Hongzhu up — one arm beneath her back, one beneath her knees — and lifted her with ease.

Zhao Hongzhu curled against his chest, tears falling steadily. One hand clutched his robe, and she shook with muffled sobs, her slight body seeming on the verge of fainting at any moment.

Fury rushed to Qin Shanyue's head — he didn't stop to ask questions. He simply lashed out with a kick at the nearest servant woman, sending her stumbling back with a sharp cry, her hand flying to her shoulder. Then he turned and carried Zhao Hongzhu into Warm Fragrance Pavilion.

Inside, the pavilion was in complete disarray. Chairs and tables had been overturned. Zhao Hongzhu's clothing and jewelry were strewn across the floor. Even the bedding had been yanked from the bed. Qin Shanyue could not find a single clear place to put his foot down. He stood holding Zhao Hongzhu amid the wreckage, with nothing but the sound of her weeping in his ears.

It was restrained weeping — the kind born of swallowed humiliation. At first it was only the faintest sound. But with every passing moment it seemed to grow — until at last it seemed as though she had no more strength to cry. She simply lay against Qin Shanyue's chest, and he held her, listening to her uneven breathing, waiting until she had gone entirely still before carrying her to his own courtyard.

Before Qin Shanyue had taken a wife, he had had his own private courtyard — Burnt Book Court, it was called. The name came from a childhood habit: he had disliked studying, and once secretly burned a set of ancient texts, pretending the books had never existed, whereupon his father had chased him all over the estate. When he came of age and was given his own courtyard, his father had given it that name, half in jest.

He brought Zhao Hongzhu to Burnt Book Court.

Burnt Book Court was staffed entirely by his own most trusted men — soldiers he had brought back from the battlefield, every one of them iron-disciplined. At his word, no one would enter. What had happened today would not happen again. He had given Zhao Hongzhu his word — he would not let anyone humiliate her again.

"Rest now. I'll be back." He set Zhao Hongzhu down on the bed, which was made up simply with clean blue cotton, then turned and walked out alone.

Zhao Hongzhu watched him through her tears as he turned and walked away. The anguish and helplessness on her face slowly dissolved, until her expression was entirely blank. She watched him go in silence.

By then the sky had already begun to darken. Outside, the last of the day's light was dying away. Qin Shanyue's back was broad and straight, nearly filling the doorway. The last scattered rays of sunlight caught the fine dust in the air and made it glitter, and Qin Shanyue walked through the fading evening light out of Burnt Book Court and into Rosy Sunset Garden, where the Old Madam resided.

The Old Madam was still awake.

She had nearly died from the shock earlier. When the elderly physician arrived and assessed her, he knew immediately that today had taken a grave toll. Bracing himself, he had administered a powerful medicine — a decoction brewed with a thousand-year-old wild ginseng root — and poured the whole thing down the Old Madam's throat in one go.

The effects of a thousand-year wild ginseng are formidable beyond measure. Pour it all down in one dose, and there are only two possible outcomes: either the body cannot withstand the force of it and dies from the medicine itself, or it wrests a few last weeks of life back from the hands of death. But the medicine would stimulate the Old Madam to her maximum capacity — at first it would make her feel vigorous and powerful, but because the dosage was so extreme, she would very soon be thrown into a state of simultaneous agitation and exhaustion, and some patients might even suffer from confused memory, behaving erratically, as though half mad.

The physician had once treated a retired official who, after consuming thousand-year ginseng, had gone for two full weeks without sleep — full of energy yet utterly exhausted at the same time — and had insisted he could recall his glorious days in office, demanding to go to the imperial palace in the middle of the night to kowtow before the Emperor. He had died in convulsions, twitching like a man savaged by wild dogs.

Had the Qin Old Madam not been truly at the brink, the physician would never have prescribed such a violent and dangerous remedy.

Though she had survived for now, the physician knew the days ahead in the Qin household would not be easy. He gave the necessary instructions quickly and left at the earliest possible moment, not daring to linger.

When Qin Shanyue arrived at Rosy Sunset Garden, he found the Qin Old Madam dressed, unusually, in a sharp and upright crimson robe, a dark red cloth band bound across her brow. The band drew the wrinkles on her face slightly upward, giving it a stern, taut look. She held no walking cane. Her eyes blazed with sharp energy, as though she had been abruptly filled with force. In her hands she gripped a blade that weighed a good dozen catties — and she was pushing through the crowd of maidservants and servants, heading toward the door with something close to ferocity.

It was the blade of the Qin Old Madam's late husband — Qin Shanyue's father, who had died in battle on the frontier.

"Mother." Qin Shanyue's chest tightened. He softened his voice by three degrees: "What is happening?"

The Old Madam's eyes blazed with a fierce light. When she saw Qin Shanyue, her rapid steps suddenly came to a halt. She seemed to study him for a moment before recognizing that this was her son.

"Shanyue!" The Old Madam's first word was a high, ringing shout that echoed through the entirety of Rosy Sunset Garden's front hall — strikingly forceful in the still, desolate night: "Come with me. We are going together to drive that little hussy out of our Qin estate! I have made up my mind — your station is high enough to be matched with a princess. Why would you burden yourself with such a lowly creature? I should never have indulged that old sentiment and let her through our door in the first place. She has truly disgraced our Qin family name!"

When Qin Shanyue heard the words "little hussy" and "lowly creature," his thick brows drew together sharply, and his tone cooled by two degrees, sharp and hard as clashing steel: "Mother, Hongzhu is also a child who grew up under your care. You know her character better than I do. After what happened, she has been suffering greatly. Why must you be so hard on her?"

The Old Madam's neck swiveled slowly in Qin Shanyue's direction, inch by inch. The deeply sunken sockets of her eyes flared with twin points of fierce light — like two blades, scraping hard against Qin Shanyue's flesh and bone.

Qin Shanyue had survived the battlefield; he was not afraid of being pressured by a woman of sixty. But there were some things he felt he could not in good conscience say, so instead he clasped his hands in a respectful posture and said: "Mother — take pity on Hongzhu. Take pity on your own son. Three years of missed chances, and I truly cannot afford to miss any more."

He wanted to take his life back to where it had been three years ago — to erase his encounter with Bai Qingli entirely, as though, from the very beginning, the only woman he had ever married was his Hongzhu.

From the moment Qin Shanyue began speaking, the Old Madam had been watching his face with an unblinking stare. When he finished, her whole face had gone crimson.

Not the ordinary red of anger or agitation — rather, it looked as though every part of her were on fire. The crimson was threaded with a dark undertone, the look of someone burning through their own blood and flesh to borrow a moment's strength. She seemed vigorous and powerful, yet at the same time somehow more shrunken — as though she were consuming herself.

"How dare you!"

The Old Madam's teeth made a grinding sound as her jaw clenched. Her hands trembled as she raised the heavy blade, her voice pitched high and ringing: "What is your station! You are the only legitimate son of the Qin family, a General of this court! Your father is enshrined in the imperial ancestral temple, and you fight wars for the nation! And what is Zhao Hongzhu — a woman who cannot even call herself chaste — and you would marry her? What you once felt for her was real, but she is now no better than filth. Why would you smear something so dirty across your own face? Let her through our doors, and people will mock you for the rest of your life!"

After all that, the Old Madam looked up to find her son standing at a distance, clasped hands not yet lowered, standing completely straight, and saying: "Mother, I understand it all. I simply want her."

The Old Madam felt something go blank inside her head.

Surge after surge of blood rushed toward the crown of her skull. Her hands and feet began to go cold, but her head seemed about to burst into flame. Qin Shanyue's figure swam before her eyes, multiplying into three, then abruptly collapsed into the small child he had once been.

In the Old Madam's memory, Qin Shanyue was still a little bundle — round and pink and soft, burrowed into the bedding and refusing to get up, until his father, just returned from drilling the troops, dragged the blankets away and told him: a man must stand tall and upright.

And Qin Shanyue had grown, day after day after day, into someone who stood tall and upright. He had his father's soldierly bearing and his father's fierce loyal heart. Though his nature was rigid, he was dependable and steady — the most dazzling young man in all the capital, a General who had wagered his life to expand the nation's borders and hold the walls and protect the people, worth ten times any pleasure-seeking young nobleman who spent his days in wine and silk.

The Old Madam had always thought of him as her greatest pride.

But the little child who used to pout and nestle into her arms was long gone. What stood before her now was a tall, powerful man who towered over her by two heads. He stood with his hands braced apart, not quite meeting her eyes as he spoke, obstinate, repeating those maddening words.

A wonderful match and a smooth and upright future were both within reach — why did he insist on being such a fool?

Her own son — and he would not listen to her. He would not listen!

The Madam felt the fire in her head blaze up, scorching through every vein and sinew. A surge of pressure shot straight to the top of her skull, and a tremendous swelling rose through half her back. From some unknown reserve she drew a burst of strength — and with it, she swung the heavy blade up and brought it slashing sideways at Qin Shanyue's head.

It happened without warning. Qin Shanyue had no chance to prepare; he could only stumble backward quickly — but the flat of the blade still caught him across the bridge of his nose. A few drops of blood flew. The Old Madam was still not satisfied. She continued to swing and hack at him with the blade, wild and without any pattern.

Qin Shanyue had no choice but to wrench the blade from her hands. But the moment it was gone, the Old Madam seized a flower pot and hurled it at him instead, then a teacup. Qin Shanyue dodged frantically and called on the servant women kneeling behind him to come and restrain the Old Madam.

This chaos lasted from midnight all the way through to the grey light of dawn. Every last servant in the household was drenched in sweat from exhaustion. Qin Shanyue himself felt his vision blurring at the edges. Yet the Old Madam showed no sign of flagging — her stream of cursing had the force to pierce the walls of Rosy Sunset Garden and carry all the way out into the gardens beyond.

That night, no one in Rosy Sunset Garden so much as touched a pillow. The entire staff tended to the Old Madam as they watched her, full of astonishing vitality, chase the young master around in circles, and the servants all found themselves losing track of what day or even year it was.

The last time Rosy Sunset Garden had been this lively was many years ago, when the young master had urinated into the Master's teacup, claiming he was offering the Master a cup of "youth tea."

It was not until the following morning that Qin Shanyue finally returned to Burnt Book Court.

The Old Madam was still carrying on, held down by several servant women with great effort and considerable coaxing. Burnt Book Court, by contrast, was quiet. But Qin Shanyue could not share a room with Zhao Hongzhu — even if they had already been intimate, they had no formal name to give it. The Old Madam's words from earlier in the night were still ringing in his ears, and he should, at least, observe some propriety. Yet outside of Burnt Book Court, he had nowhere else to go.

Warm Fragrance Pavilion had been ransacked and was not yet put to rights. Rosy Sunset Garden was in utter disarray. The Qin estate had other courtyards, but they had been uninhabited for years and were untouched and unswept. He wandered alone through the courtyard, and with a certain cold decisiveness, thought of how just a few days ago he had ordered the maidservants to pull up all the lotus plants in the Lotus Courtyard. After Zhao Hongzhu's wedding, he would have the pond filled in entirely and the Lotus Courtyard sealed off. In a few years, he would turn it into something else — erasing every last trace Bai Qingli had left behind.

So when Qin Shanyue entered the Lotus Courtyard now, all he saw was a body of still water — not a single lotus in sight. The fish inside, with no one to feed them, had long since starved to death. Only a few small frogs were still hopping about noisily. The entire Lotus Courtyard was as silent as something already dead.

Qin Shanyue stood at the entrance and felt, abruptly, a wave of loneliness.

He followed the familiar path to their bedroom. The room he had shared with Bai Qingli was still as it had been — simply and elegantly furnished. Only the vase was empty.

Bai Qingli had always loved flowers. No matter what time of year, the vase would always hold a bouquet suited to the season. Now, in late September bordering on October, it should have held chrysanthemums — most likely vibrant yellow daisies, five or six blooms fitted through the narrow neck of the vase, each one carefully trimmed, set by the window to catch the morning sun and bloom freely.

Qin Shanyue looked at the empty vase, looked at the dim and quiet room, and finally dropped heavily onto the yellow rosewood canopy bed.

The bedding hadn't been changed in two or three days. Qin Shanyue didn't mind. On the battlefield, when he was utterly spent, he would sleep on the ground beside his soldiers — blood and sweat, earth and grass, sometimes finding a worm or a snake on him when he woke. This simple, spare bed was, by comparison, more than adequate.

When he lay down, he had expected his churning thoughts to keep him awake. But as soon as he turned his head, he was plunged into deep sleep.

He fell into that same strange dream as before — and in the dream, once again, he was Bai Qingli.

This time, the dream had advanced to the night of the banquet. From inside Bai Qingli's body, he witnessed with his own eyes the secret meeting between Qin Shanyue and Zhao Hongzhu in that side room — and suffered the casual, dismissive jabs of Lancao's words — and felt his chest twist with anguish and fury. Then he watched, helpless, as Qiuyue was falsely accused of stealing and condemned to death.

Trapped in Bai Qingli's body within the dream, Qin Shanyue felt with absolute clarity her bitterness and her grief. And when Qiuyue died, even Qin Shanyue — a mere observer — was swept up in the storm of it.

He was still adrift in the dream when a familiar voice reached him.

Qin Shanyue opened his bleary eyes with effort and found it was one of his subordinates, who had clasped his fists in salute and was saying: "General — a summons has arrived from the palace."

His drowsiness vanished at once. He heaved himself upright from the bed, though his movements were, somehow, strangely sluggish as he climbed down.

This dream — it connected with the last one. Every detail so vivid that it felt less like a dream and more like something that had actually happened at some point in time.

He couldn't make sense of it. He kept telling himself it was only a dream — but it was too strange. What dream stayed so real, and continued like a serial story, rising and falling in his mind as though it were a novel playing itself out?

Something heavy seemed to be suspended over his heart. Qin Shanyue had a vague but persistent sense of foreboding that he could not quite name.

"General?" His subordinate called again, puzzled.

A summons from His Majesty — urgent beyond measure — and the General was standing there in a daze?

"Yes." Qin Shanyue came back to himself, rose, quickly put himself in order, and walked out the door.

Before leaving the Qin estate, he made sure to instruct the men of Burnt Book Court: do not allow the Old Madam or the Old Madam's servants to enter Burnt Book Court. Guard Zhao Hongzhu well. His word was as good as a military order — no one would be allowed past the gates.

What had happened yesterday would not happen again. He had given Zhao Hongzhu his word.

* * *

Compared to the Qin estate, Bai Qingli's situation was considerably more tranquil.

The previous day she had drunk herself into a stupor and simply collapsed onto the bed. By the time she woke, it was already the following day. She rose with an aching all over — from too much wine, most likely — her head still swimming, unsteady on her feet and having to hold onto the wall to walk.

The first thing she saw upon coming out was Qiuyue looking at her with an expression of exasperated disappointment, in an oddly leading tone of voice: "Mistress — shall we draw a bath?"

After all that wine yesterday, her body felt sticky and unpleasant, so naturally a bath was needed. Bai Qingli nodded. She had been about to add "and heat some water for tea while you're at it," but Qiuyue had already bolted out the door like a gust of wind before the words were out.

Chun Ri had been waiting at the kitchen door for a gossip session, and Bai Qingli settled back to rest while the water heated. A little while later, Chun Ri brought tea and they got down to business.

"What news has come back in recent days?"

Bai Qingli was asking about the Bai and Qin households. On the Bai family's side, Chun Ri had bribed two loose-tongued maidservants with a generous sum of silver to gather information. On the Qin family's side, Chun Ri had gleaned information from some of her former acquaintances in the Qin household.

"Nothing too dramatic from the Bai family."

By now Chun Ri was fully aware of what Bai Qingli had done, and regarded her with an extra measure of awe. She served the tea with great care, speaking as she poured: "The Bai family's master has been frequenting the wine houses and entertainment districts and hasn't gone home at all. The First Young Master is said to have been reprimanded again. The Bai Madam has been locking herself in her room every day, not daring to go out. It seems she hasn't told either of the Bai men about the terrible tumble she took, or perhaps she's just watching to see how the Qin household responds. Either way — nothing has erupted."

Bai Qingli sipped her tea. Good well water properly boiled, fresh tea leaves — the fragrance was clean and sweet. She took one sip, then heard Chun Ri move on to the Qin household.

"The Qin household made quite a spectacular scene."

Chun Ri had spent so much time around Qiuyue lately that her own manner had loosened considerably. She could barely contain her excitement as she recounted the tale, her tone full of relish.

Spring had left the Fog Forest Courtyard that morning, spending fifteen copper coins on a cart from the village, rode all the way to the city market, and tracked down two local fixers under cover of a veil. At no small expense, she had paid them to spread a rumor.

The content of the rumor was simple enough.

The young Miss Zhao had returned to the capital — though her family's fortunes were ruined, she still carried herself with elegance, and her beauty was enough to overturn cities and nations. First she had lured the great General Qin Shanyue — her childhood sweetheart — into dismissing his wife to prepare for marriage to her. Then she had ensnared Bai Yunhe, Vice Minister of Justice, at first sight, sparking enmity between Qin Shanyue and Bai Yunhe and souring the relationship between the Qin and Bai families. Madam Bai had personally gone to the Qin estate to propose a marriage for her son with Zhao Hongzhu, but the Qin Old Madam, who regarded Zhao Hongzhu as a daughter, had flatly refused, and the two women had come to blows — with the result that the Old Madam was left gravely ill and had nearly died on the spot.

The story sounded outlandish on its own — but the more outlandish a rumor, the faster and further it travels. And, fatally, part of it was true.

There had also been whispers drifting out from both the Qin and Bai estates in recent days; anyone with the inclination to dig a little had turned up a few threads of fact — and once truth and invention were braided together, they became impossible to separate. Within a single day, this scandal of two men contending for one woman had spread across every corner of the capital like wildfire, reaching even the most remote villages. When Qiuyue wandered to the village nearest Fog Forest Courtyard out of boredom, she overheard village women laundering clothes by the stream, chattering merrily about the affairs of the great houses.

The story grew wilder in each retelling. Before long, people were saying the Zhao girl was a hundred-year fox spirit who had taken human form; that any man who so much as laid eyes on her would have his soul snatched away and become her devoted slave forever.

Qiuyue listened in total astonishment. Her own daily life had become someone else's talking point, and the version they were telling was so vivid and specific that it stirred even her. When had Zhao Hongzhu gotten involved with the First Young Master of the Bai family? How had she managed not to hear a word of this?

Qiuyue had been raised as a household servant from birth in the Bai family, had known the First Young Master Bai since childhood, and had then entered the Qin household and come to know Qin Shanyue. Now the First Young Master Bai was apparently competing with General Qin over the same woman — it made her feel as though her entire understanding of reality had somehow gone wrong.

She made her way back to Fog Forest Courtyard with a head full of bewilderment and gossip. She had thought to ask the mistress about it, then worried that hearing such things would hurt her — both the First Young Master Bai and General Qin were closely connected to the mistress, after all. So she decided to wait until Chun Ri returned from the market and share the news with her instead.

Chun Ri had been chopping meat at the time — she'd gone out that day and brought back two jin of pork ribs, cut two strips of well-marbled pork belly, and bought several bundles of fresh vegetables, planning to make a good meal. When Qiuyue came in bursting to tell her something, Chun Ri assumed she'd been eavesdropping on the mistress and the kept man, and immediately perked up with interest: "What is it?"

Qiuyue held up two fingers with a solemn expression: "You have to promise me you won't tell a single person."

Chun Ri's curiosity intensified. She set down the cleaver and raised one meat-oil-smeared finger to mirror the pledge.

Qiuyue glanced around the kitchen doorway and window with a theatrically conspiratorial air, making sure no one was nearby. Then she crouched down next to Chun Ri, assuming her most dramatic posture, and only when Chun Ri leaned close did she say: "The First Young Master Bai — you know him? He's gotten involved with Zhao Hongzhu!"

The expectant expression on Chun Ri's face slowly congealed.

Those words sounded oddly familiar. Like something that had come out of her own mouth just that morning.

Qiuyue continued, gesturing enthusiastically as she spoke: "And on top of that, Madam Bai went personally to the Qin estate to arrange the marriage between Zhao Hongzhu and her son — guess what happened next?"

Chun Ri pressed her lips together, stepped back to the chopping board, and began chopping meat again.

She could not believe she had actually sat there listening to Qiuyue's nonsense. What could Qiuyue possibly know?

Seeing Chun Ri stop responding, Qiuyue grew frantic — she had a belly full of tremendous secrets and no audience, and there was simply no holding it in! If Chun Ri wouldn't ask, she'd just circle around behind her and pester: "Guess! Come on, guess!"

Chun Ri's cleaver hit the board with a satisfying series of thuds, the pork belly being reduced to neat square blocks. She kept chopping, and said with deliberate boredom: "I can't guess."

Qiuyue couldn't hold back any longer and blurted it out: "The Old Madam nearly got herself worked up to death!"

Chun Ri gave a deadpan response of "How surprising," but inwardly she was marveling quietly at the mistress's prescience.

The rumor that had left her own mouth just this morning, and by evening — the sun barely having set — it was already coming back to her through Qiuyue's lips. The rumor had clearly swept through every street and alley in the city.

Qiuyue only knew how to watch the excitement from the sidelines. She'd heard a rumor and come straight home to repeat it, without the slightest awareness of what sort of enormous wave those few sentences would send crashing through the capital.

Zhao Hongzhu's reputation was ruined from this day forward. She was already the daughter of a condemned traitor who had returned from exile — every great household in the capital regarded her with some degree of wariness, watching to see how she would conduct herself going forward. And now she had first become entangled in an ambiguous relationship with Qin Shanyue, a married man, and then gotten mixed up with Bai Yunhe on top of that. How was that any different from the women who worked in pleasure houses?

As for the relationship between the Bai and Qin families — it was finished. They had become the laughingstock of the entire capital. Both households were families of standing and consequence; going forward, they would never be able to fully shake each other off. Like two strips of dog-skin plaster stuck together — at the sight of each other they would be irritated, yet they would remain adhesively, inextricably joined, and no amount of pulling could separate them.

Qin Shanyue was one thing — he had chosen of his own stubborn will to marry Zhao Hongzhu, and surely had long since considered these consequences. But Bai Yunhe had truly been struck by lightning out of a clear sky. He was just half a year away from marrying his superior's noble daughter. The Bai family's foundations were thin; Bai Yunhe had put enormous effort into making himself worthy in the eyes of the Minister of Justice — he didn't so much as keep a maidservant as a concubine, had even sworn to take no second wife in his lifetime, all of which had delighted the Minister and prompted him to help pave the way for a smooth and promising career. A clear and bright future had been within Bai Yunhe's reach — and now this had appeared, and the Bai household was in an uproar as well.

Words, too, can kill.

"Chun Ri, are you even listening to me!"
