Qiuyue had just gotten to the part about Zhao Hongzhu possibly being a reincarnated fox spirit when she looked up and found Chun Ri lost in thought over her chopping, apparently far more interested in the meat on the board than in anything Qiuyue was saying. She stamped her foot in indignation, cried "I'm ignoring you!" and made to run out — then got called back by Chun Ri to pick over the vegetables.

"No vegetable picking, no dinner tonight!"

The two young maidservants bickered and chattered, the small kitchen warm and smoky with the smell of an ordinary evening meal. In the study of Fog Forest Courtyard, an oil lamp was lit. An autumn breeze stirred the air. The sun hung distantly behind a tall mountain, sinking lazily downward, its orange light painting the sky into a sweep of evening color. The rivers lay gentle, and the world was soft and warm.

* * *

When Qiuyue came to call Bai Qingli to the front hall for dinner, Bai Qingli was pulling on a rough-woven hemp skirt.

The skirt was newly made — the style plain and ordinary, the fabric one of the cheapest available. Qiuyue had grown up in the Bai household and had never worn cloth of this quality. The sight of Bai Qingli pulling it on made her eyes go wide in shock.

Had their mistress truly fallen so low?

Since leaving the General's estate, they did indeed seem to be rather short of money — and they had a male fox-spirit to support!

Was it because she, Qiuyue, had been eating too much? Was the mistress unable to afford to feed her anymore?

"What is it?" Bai Qingli, catching sight of Qiuyue's expression, casually picked up a sash from the table. It was more of a cloth rope than a sash — a long strip of cut fabric that she wound around her waist a few times and knotted.

Qiuyue's nose went red.

When their young mistress had been unmarried in the Bai household, she had worn sashes woven of pure silk. After marrying into the Qin estate, she had used a golden sash set with South Sea pearls, woven by master craftsmen from gold thread and pearls. The mistress never particularly favored the golden sashes, preferring plain ones in simple silver thread — but even those silver thread sashes had a different style and different embroidered patterns every single day. When had she ever worn something like this?

"What's the matter?" Bai Qingli asked in surprise, following up: "Why are you crying? Who has wronged you?"

There were only four people in the whole courtyard, and every one of them was easy to get along with. Surely she hadn't been wronged out in the village?

"Nothing." Qiuyue dragged the sleeve across her eyes, and when she looked up, her expression was resolute: "Mistress! Your servant swears — your servant will never eat dinner again. Or snacks either!"

Before Bai Qingli could even ask "what does your crying have to do with not eating dinner," Qiuyue had already turned and dashed out.

Bai Qingli had no choice but to go to the front hall on her own.

In the front hall, Shen Shizhuo was sitting alone, upright in his seat. Chun Ri had set out the dishes and, with a bow, excused herself.

Back in the Qin estate, dining had involved a degree of formality. But at Fog Forest Courtyard, Bai Qingli did as she pleased — she often invited Chun Ri and Qiuyue to eat at the table with her and Shen Shizhuo. Today, however, Qiuyue had inexplicably run off, and Chun Ri felt that Shen Shizhuo's position was somewhat special and that it wouldn't do to overstep, so she ate alone in the small kitchen. Which left only the two of them.

Shen Shizhuo had been raised in a temple, but his wet nurse had taught him proper manners from infancy — one does not speak while eating or sleeping. He would not sit down before Bai Qingli arrived; he simply sat properly upright in his chair.

He wore only a plain scholar's robe. Qiuyue had given his clothing and general care very little thought and had bought him the most basic off-the-shelf garments from a ready-made clothes shop, with no ornamentation whatsoever — a single color head to toe. The fabric, on closer inspection, didn't quite fit; the sleeves were somewhat too wide, and he had folded them back, leaving a length of wrist visible. He had no hair ornament either, only a wooden pin to hold his hair. Yet his face was remarkable enough — bright and luminous as the moon — that none of this made him look shabby. On the contrary, he wore it all with an air of someone who had dined on mist and drunk from the wind, an otherworldly quality, like a solitary crane in the mountains.

When he saw Bai Qingli, a brief flicker passed through Shen Shizhuo's phoenix eyes.

Every other time he had seen her, she had been dressed in robes of golden silk thread and silver-jade hairpins — like an immortal descended from the highest heavens, her hem trailing behind her as she walked in a cloud of lotus blossoms, the corners of her eyes carrying that cool, untouchable elegance. Today she was entirely different — rough cotton wrapped around her slender waist, tracing the graceful lines of her figure; the silver pins and elaborate hair arrangements replaced by a simple circle tied with a length of blue cord cut from the same cloth as her sash, no ornamentation anywhere. In the flickering orange candlelight, she seemed to glow from within, warm as jade.

Less cool and remote — and somehow more vivid. She looked, somehow, as though she had become several years younger all at once.

"Shall we eat?" Bai Qingli said as she sat down. "We'll be going out tonight."

Shen Shizhuo picked up his chopsticks, but his heart was hammering.

She was... asking him out?

The moon rises above the willow tips; in the dusk they had made their appointment.

They were living under the same roof, but with two maidservants always about, it really wasn't the right setting for romantic outings.

He had no personal experience in the affairs of men and women, but the young men at the pleasure house had accompanied patrons on outings before. When they returned, they would say that when an ordinary woman and a man had settled their intentions toward each other, they would go out to some scenic, secluded place and spend the day there — and some of the men had been invited out for several days at a time, returning with the patron practically having to carry them back on arrival.

His thoughts had wandered somewhere entirely unexpected. Shen Shizhuo's ears were red enough to bleed. The moment Bai Qingli set down her chopsticks, he was immediately on his feet.

Bai Qingli took a sip of tea, then rose and walked out with Shen Shizhuo.

They went by carriage — she had Shen Shizhuo drive them to West Street in the outer city of the capital.

The capital was divided into an inner city and an outer city. Neither had a curfew, but once night fell, the gates between them were closed and no one could pass between them. The inner city was inhabited mostly by nobles and officials, every inch of it valuable. The outer city was mostly ordinary commoners, and West Street was a mixed and lively place where people of all trades and backgrounds made their way.

Shen Shizhuo had grown up on the mountain and been brought into the pleasure house after coming down. Though he was sharp and alert by nature, his dealings with the people of the capital were limited. He knew where West Street was, but had no clear idea of what specifically went on there. Bai Qingli, for her part, was more familiar with the place.

Since her rebirth, Bai Qingli had been actively exploring every possible means of securing a path forward for herself. She had gone into every sort of rough and mixed neighborhood. She had money — and when you scattered enough silver, every door could be opened.

Shen Shizhuo drove the carriage from Fog Forest Courtyard to West Street in about half an hour, finally pulling up in front of a tea house at Bai Qingli's direction.

The capital had no curfew, so West Street blazed with light from one end to the other. With no constables on duty at night, the street was full of all manner of characters — women in gauze hats moving quickly through the crowd, drunkards with wine jars and leering eyes, finely dressed customers, wandering martial figures in warrior's dress. A living tapestry of humanity.

The moment the carriage stopped, Shen Shizhuo noticed several gazes settling on him.

He had trained in martial arts since childhood and was acutely sensitive to hostile attention from his surroundings. His back straightened, and his fingertips closed around a small hidden dagger.

This did not appear to be a place suited for a romantic outing.

Just then, Bai Qingli drew back the carriage curtain.

She wore no powder or rouge — her clean, fair face caught the moonlight and seemed to glow. As she descended from the carriage, she naturally placed her hand on Shen Shizhuo's arm. The carriage came up to her waist; as she stepped down, her weight naturally shifted onto Shen Shizhuo's side.

Like throwing herself into his arms.

Shen Shizhuo's heart turned over. The wine-scent drifting from a nearby drunkard seemed suddenly intoxicating, as though he were about to be drunk to death in the middle of all the blazing lanterns.

Whether or not this was a place for a romantic outing, they were on a romantic outing right now. Even with ten blades at their throats, they would still be on a romantic outing.

"This way." Bai Qingli paid no attention to Shen Shizhuo's reaction. She didn't particularly mind physical closeness with him.

When they had lived together in the snowy mountains and the old Qin estate — when she had been so ill she was nearly dying, with no capable maidservants to tend to her — Shen Shizhuo had managed all of her daily needs. At first she had been flustered and embarrassed. But after staring death in the face enough times, such things stopped mattering. She had simply come to think of Shen Shizhuo as her closest companion, no different from Qiuyue.

"You — what are we here for?"

Shen Shizhuo had wanted to call her "Qingli" — but it felt too intimate, as though his tongue had caught fire and he couldn't get the words out. Anything else felt off somehow, so he settled for the vaguely noncommittal "you."

"Call me Aning." Bai Qingli was more at ease than he was — she took his arm in hers, and they walked inside together, pressed close, though her voice remained cool and even without the slightest flutter of shyness: "I'm Wang Ning, and you're Zhao Shi. We're a newly married couple, here to buy identity tablets and travel documents."

An identity tablet was what people of the time used to prove who they were. Every law-abiding person had one; each person's identity was recorded on the tablet and registered against the official records of their local government office. If you traveled to another region, you needed your tablet as proof of identity — without it, you could not settle elsewhere, buy land, or open a shop. Travel documents contained your personal history — how many people in the household, how many acres of land in the village, and so forth.

Bai Qingli naturally had her own identity tablet. But she could no longer use the identity of Bai Qingli — she had made enemies of both the Qin and Bai families, and feared retribution from both sides. Shen Shizhuo had never had an identity tablet to begin with. Bai Qingli's plan was simply to have two new ones made and start over somewhere else entirely.

West Street in the outer city was exactly where this kind of business was conducted, away from the light. Given enough money, they could fabricate two complete people out of thin air — full names, ancestry, place of origin — as though those two people had always existed. Posing as a married couple made it convenient, and later, Qiuyue and Chun Ri could be presented as their younger sisters.

Shen Shizhuo walked arm in arm with Bai Qingli into the tea house, thinking in a daze: she said she and I are husband and wife.

She had to pretend to be his wife just to buy an identity tablet. She truly... cannot help herself when it comes to me.

* * *

A young servant came forward with a bright smile when they entered the tea house and asked: "Red tea or green tea for the two of you?"

The tea house did two kinds of business: red tea meant buying and selling information about the capital; green tea meant the production of identity tablets.

"Green tea."

"Right this way."

The servant led them into a private room, poured two cups of plain tea, and withdrew. Within moments, an old man appeared. He produced the identity tablets for them on the spot and recorded their registered ancestry.

"In half a month, these two tablets will be ready for use. As long as no one deliberately investigates the ancestral records of these two tablets, they should cause no trouble." The old man smiled pleasantly: "Is there anything else you'd like to know?"

Bai Qingli considered, then slid the silver she'd prepared across the table: "Some red tea."

Red tea meant she wanted information.

She intended to ask about Zhao Hongzhu and Qin Shanyue. The intelligence Chun Ri could gather was limited. From her own memory, the Zhao family's case would soon be reversed, and Zhao Hongzhu's fortunes would turn within the next few days. Bai Qingli wanted to know — after the rumor had spread — how Zhao Hongzhu was faring in the Qin household.

The old man smiled: "Please wait a moment, Miss."

When the old man left, the person who came in next was a slight young man of around seventeen or eighteen, with the sharp, shifty look of someone who kept to the shadows. His eyes lit up when he smiled.

Clearly, this tea house had different people handling different parts of the business.

"What kind of tea would Miss like?" the sharp-eyed young man asked, and at the same time slid over a stack of blank paper and a brush loaded with ink, drawing out an iron basin from behind him, dropping two pieces of wood into it, and striking a spark with a flint.

Bai Qingli picked up the brush and wrote two names on the white paper: Zhao Hongzhu and Zhao clan. Then: Qin Shanyue.

The sharp-eyed young man thought for a moment, made a gesture with his fingers, and once Bai Qingli had counted out the corresponding silver, he wrote quickly on the paper in a few swift lines.

"The Zhao clan's fortunes are about to turn. Within the next few days."

"Qin Shanyue has petitioned the Emperor to issue an imperial decree of marriage for him and Zhao Hongzhu."

Bai Qingli read it and gave a cold, slight curl of her lips.

Qin Shanyue, going so far to give Zhao Hongzhu a face — he truly had no shame. Zhao Hongzhu had already become someone every passerby in the street would gladly spit on, and yet he was personally petitioning the Emperor for a marriage decree. A decree from the Emperor would make the union a matter of imperial prestige — even if Zhao Hongzhu had lapses of private virtue, no one would dare say a word.

But none of this had anything to do with her anymore.

The grudges of her previous life — repaid through those two deaths and everything that had happened since — were now fully settled. From this point on, they had nothing to do with each other.

She tossed the paper into the iron basin. The flames consumed both sheets in an instant, and she watched the past reduce to ash. Bai Qingli rose, took Shen Shizhuo by the arm, and left the private room.

The tea was finished. It was time to go.

When they left the tea house, Shen Shizhuo helped Bai Qingli into the carriage, then climbed up to drive them home.

On the way back, the names "Qin Shanyue" and "Zhao Hongzhu" floated through Shen Shizhuo's mind.

He knew little of the affairs of the Da Feng court — Qin Shanyue he had heard of occasionally; Zhao Hongzhu he had never heard of at all. But when he had watched Bai Qingli write down those two names, and seen the cold light carefully tucked away in the depths of her eyes — he couldn't stop wondering: who were these two people? What was their connection to Bai Qingli? He could not bring himself to ask, because he too was carrying a belly full of secrets — about his own past, his own origins. And yet Bai Qingli had never once asked.

Did Bai Qingli not find him at all curious?

The road home was dark and quiet, only the moon above lighting their way, not a soul anywhere around them. Something inside Shen Shizhuo's heart was like a cat pawing and scratching at him without pause.

There were so many things about Bai Qingli he wanted to know.

The road home was so long — why wouldn't she come out and say something? Something that would make it feel more natural for him to ask.

The cat scratched harder and harder. Shen Shizhuo's palms had grown damp against the reins. Several times on the journey he had nearly opened his mouth — and each time, the moment had slipped away.

The horse trotted the whole way back to Fog Forest Courtyard. The carriage had only just come to a stop when Bai Qingli lifted the curtain and said quietly: "The moonlight is beautiful tonight."

Bai Qingli took Shen Shizhuo's arm and stepped down. On hearing his words, she looked up naturally at the moon.

It was the tenth month; the capital air was cold. But the moon hung as bright as ever — clear and luminous against the clouds, surrounded on all sides by the silver radiance of attending stars.

"It is beautiful," Bai Qingli agreed.

She didn't notice: when she said those words, Shen Shizhuo's arm had loosely circled her waist, drawing himself up slightly to make it easier for her to lean on him as she descended. When she tilted her head back to look at the moon, the moonlight fell across her face — and from close, close beside her, Shen Shizhuo gazed down at her.

She was looking at the moon. Shen Shizhuo was looking at her. The moonlight adorned her jade face; and she adorned Shen Shizhuo's dreams.

* * *

Walking in from the Fog Forest Courtyard gate, turning down the small path toward the rooms, Shen Shizhuo's heart was entirely submerged in warm water. He felt the lingering warmth of her in his hand, the impression of her slight figure still curled against his chest, and his normally steady, composed steps felt as though they might drift off the ground.

And so it was that as he passed the kitchen, he failed to hear those faint footsteps — until a heavier landing sound reached him, and he wheeled around sharply.

"Who's there?"

In the moonlight, a rough, weathered face emerged. The man from before — the one who had come to the study earlier. He said quietly: "Young Master, the situation has become very dangerous. I fear the threat is about to reach the Young Master directly. Your residence here is no longer safe. Today, several scouts located the Young Master's whereabouts — this subordinate has dealt with all of them. If the Young Master remains here any longer, I am afraid it will bring danger to the women in the household—"

Shen Shizhuo tensed at the warning but stiffened when he heard the words "the women in the household."

He was not afraid for himself. If assassins came, he could hold them off. But the other women — if they came face to face with such people, not one of them would survive. Chun Ri and Qiuyue were both utterly loyal to Bai Qingli, and Bai Qingli regarded them both as sisters. If even one of them died, Bai Qingli would be devastated.

If it happened because of him, he feared Bai Qingli would come to resent him for it.

But he also did not dare reveal to Bai Qingli the murky tangle of his origins. He was afraid Bai Qingli would be frightened, or burdened.

Who would not be frightened by assassins that could arrive without warning? Who could withstand the constant fear of a blade at one's throat in the night? If Bai Qingli grew tired of him or came to dislike him because of all this — what could he do?

Bai Qingli had grown tired of her previous husband and had dissolved the marriage and changed her identity entirely, making herself impossible to find. If she did the same to him—

The man noticed that his words were having some effect, and quickly added: "Young Master, circumstances move quickly — a new development every day. You know, the Master has been walking on thin ice all these years, and things have only been growing harder—"

The man had only gotten that far when a voice drifted over, thick with sleepiness.

"Shen Shizhuo, who is this person?"

Both Shen Shizhuo and the man startled at once. They spun around, eyes sweeping to the side — and there was Qiuyue, roused from sleep in the middle of the night, standing by a tree and looking at them in muddled confusion.

Qiuyue had been woken by hunger. She hadn't eaten dinner, and had spent the whole night dreaming of gnawing on a pork knuckle, the discomfort eventually dragging her out of bed.

Shen Shizhuo hadn't yet figured out how to explain any of this to Bai Qingli. So when Qiuyue asked "who is this person" a second time, Shen Shizhuo blurted out: "A friend of mine."

The man kept cautiously silent, standing in place and letting Qiuyue look him over.

The moment Qiuyue heard the words "a friend of Shen Shizhuo's," her neat little brows drew together: "He looks like a poor wretch."

Shen Shizhuo, catching up belatedly to the man's recent line about "things growing harder and harder," replied: "That's right — he came to borrow money. I'll send him on his way shortly. Qiuyue, I'd appreciate it if you didn't mention this... to her."

Qiuyue gave a cold sniff, and seeing Shen Shizhuo's careful, apologetic manner, felt she had caught hold of something she could use against him. She became immediately imperious — swept her gaze from Shen Shizhuo's face to the man's, looked him up and down with critical disapproval, lifted her round chin, and said with full disdain: "Someone like you being poor is perfectly normal."

The man couldn't understand why she would say that. He was of humble birth, yes, but his martial skills were exceptional — vigorous, powerful, a seasoned fighter who had put his life on the line for years and was greatly valued. How could she call him poor?

Qiuyue continued, answering her own question: "A man like you — you probably couldn't get a single patron at the pleasure house, could you? Tsk. Ugly and dark. If I were a patron, I wouldn't pick you. Look at that face — you must be forty. That old, and anyone still willing to look at you?"

The man's face went instantly crimson, his chest so tight it felt about to burst.

Qiuyue turned her fire on Shen Shizhuo: "And another thing — the mistress can barely keep the pot boiling! Haven't you noticed me tightening my own belt? What are you doing running around with this rabble of yours? Eating and drinking and spending at the mistress's expense, and now handing out money on top of it? What exactly do you have to offer besides what you do in bed? In the future, stop trying to compete with me for the mistress's favor — I'm the one who truly understands her, who the mistress values most!"

This fox-spirit of a man did nothing but take the mistress's silver to show off to others. Only she — only she — was the maidservant truly devoted to her mistress, who for the mistress's sake was willing to go a whole night without eating!

Surely that loyalty earned her the right to help herself to a small midnight snack?

Having delivered her tirade, Qiuyue was no longer sleepy at all — invigorated, she walked into the kitchen and cooked herself a private meal. Shen Shizhuo led the man, whose temples were visibly throbbing with suppressed fury, away at a swift pace.

Once they were clear of the kitchen, Shen Shizhuo said: "Tell me what the current situation is. Let me consider it."

chapters.title: Thirty (repeated chapter)
chapters.content:
(TL: this chapter seems to be a repeat, but I am still going to post it, cause this is the only chapter 30 I have seen, but you can skip it,)

Shen Shizhuo stood frozen in the doorway, not knowing what to do.

From inside, Bai Qingli called out again: "Come help me knead my shoulders."

Shen Shizhuo didn't know that Bai Qingli was calling for Qiuyue. He assumed she was calling for him — after all, they had now exchanged formal vows, and though they hadn't yet shared a bridal chamber, they had drunk the wedding wine together; their commitment to each other was sealed. Delivering a cloth and kneading her shoulders seemed, he supposed, entirely within reason.

Shen Shizhuo walked into the space behind the bathing screen, one foot moving before the other in anxious disarray.

Bai Qingli had her back to him, leaning against the rim of the bathing tub. Her dark hair fell in loose, silk-smooth cascades, her bare shoulders round and soft — a vision, at first glance, of ink clouds and white snow.

Shen Shizhuo's throat went dry. He fixed his eyes on the lines of the floorboards. He pulled a cloth from the screen, handed it to Bai Qingli, then took a second cloth, soaked it in water, laid it over Bai Qingli's shoulders, and pressed his hands down from behind.

His palms were broad and strong, but the pressure he applied was perfectly calibrated — enough to ease the tension from the muscles and joints without causing pain. Through the warm wet cloth, the flesh and bone underneath softened and released, and a pleasant warmth spread through the whole body.

He worked not only the shoulders and neck but also the pressure points on her head. His hands moved through her thick, sleek hair and pressed against her scalp with a noticeably firmer touch than at her shoulders — firm enough that Bai Qingli felt a spreading tingle of heat and numbness through her scalp, a particular kind of deep comfort that made one want to sink into the bed and sleep through the night. Bai Qingli went limp and languid, leaning backward with her hair nearly brushing against Shen Shizhuo's long robe — and the contact set his heart pounding.

He only had to lower his head to see the ripples in the water below. He did not dare lower his head. His eyes went to the ceiling, the window, the wood grain, the flowers, the clouds, the sky — taking in every corner of the sparsely furnished room and the wide expanse of the world beyond — and yet his heartbeat refused to slow.

Only when Bai Qingli drifted back to sleep against the side of the tub did Shen Shizhuo stop. His back was damp with sweat. He still didn't dare lower his head — he kept his rigid posture and stepped, inch by careful inch, out of the room. Then he went outside and found Qiuyue eating a snack.

"Stop eating. She... has fallen asleep in the bathtub. Go and wake her up."

The autumn air was cold, and the water cooled quickly. Sleeping in the water would easily lead to catching a chill, and given Bai Qingli's constitution, a chill would take at least half a month to recover from.

"Fine," Qiuyue said. She hadn't wanted to bother with him, but on second thought — these days Shen Shizhuo was rather more in the mistress's favor than she was. She was nothing but yesterday's news. In the end, a small maidservant like her couldn't compete with a fox-spirit who knew how to warm a bed. He might even whisper bad things about her to the mistress later. The more she thought about it, the more disadvantaged she felt, and so she grudgingly let her temper go, got up with great reluctance, and went to wake the mistress.

* * *

The clumsy maidservant crashed into the room, the wooden door banging with a loud thud. The sound carried far, dissolving among the pine-green trees, while in the distance the golden light of the sky traced the edges of white clouds, and nearby the branches were thick and full of life. Fog Forest Courtyard lay wrapped in a quiet like the gentle passage of years.

Meanwhile, Chun Ri had slipped out from the courtyard that morning, hired a village cart for fifteen copper coins, and rode it all the way to the market in the city. With her face partly covered, she tracked down two local fixers and paid them a generous sum to spread a rumor.

The content was simple enough.

The former Miss Zhao had returned to the capital — though her family's fortunes were ruined, she still carried herself with grace, and her beauty was enough to topple cities. First she had entranced General Qin Shanyue, her childhood sweetheart, into dismissing his wife and preparing to take her instead. Then she had captivated Bai Yunhe, the Vice Minister of Justice, on first sight, drawing enmity between Qin Shanyue and Bai Yunhe and souring relations between the Qin and Bai families. Madam Bai had gone personally to the Qin estate to petition for Zhao Hongzhu's marriage into the Bai family, but the Qin Old Madam, who regarded Zhao Hongzhu as her own daughter, had flatly refused and come to blows with Madam Bai, resulting in the Old Madam falling gravely ill and nearly dying on the spot.

The story sounded outlandish at first hearing — but the more outlandish a rumor, the faster and wider it travels. And, crucially, part of it was true.

There had also been some wind drifting out from both the Qin and Bai estates recently — anyone inclined to look further would find enough threads of fact that, once truth and fiction were woven together, no one could separate them. In less than a day, this tale of two men vying for one woman spread through the entire capital as though it had grown wings, reaching even the most secluded hamlets. When Qiuyue wandered to the village nearest Fog Forest Courtyard for something to do, she overheard village women scrubbing laundry at the stream and chattering merrily about the affairs of the great houses.

With every retelling it grew more extravagant — before long, people were saying the Zhao girl was a hundred-year fox spirit who had taken human form, and that any man who so much as caught a glimpse of her would have his soul snatched away and become her devoted slave forever.

Qiuyue stood there with her jaw on the ground. Her own daily life had become other people's gossip, and the version they were telling was so vivid and detailed that even she was caught up in it. When had Zhao Hongzhu gotten involved with the First Young Master of the Bai family? She had somehow never heard a word of this.

Qiuyue had grown up as a household servant in the Bai family and had known the First Young Master Bai since childhood, then entered the Qin household and come to know Qin Shanyue. And now the First Young Master Bai was apparently competing with General Qin for the same woman — it made her feel as though her entire grasp of reality had somehow gone wrong.

She made her way back to Fog Forest Courtyard with a head full of bewilderment and gossip. She had thought to ask the mistress — then worried that such a story might cause the mistress pain, since both the First Young Master Bai and the General were closely connected to her. So she waited until Chun Ri came back from the market and told her instead.

Chun Ri had been chopping meat at the time. She'd gone out that day and come back with two jin of pork ribs, cut two pieces of well-marbled pork belly, and bought several bundles of fresh vegetables, planning to make a good meal. Hearing Qiuyue want to tell her something, she assumed Qiuyue had been eavesdropping on the mistress and the kept man, and immediately perked up: "What is it?"

Qiuyue held up two fingers with a solemn air: "You have to swear you won't tell a single person."

Chun Ri's curiosity deepened. She set down the cleaver and raised one meat-oil-smeared finger in pledge.

Qiuyue cast a theatrically cautious glance around the kitchen doorway and window to make sure no one was about, then crouched down next to Chun Ri, assumed her full conspiratorial posture, and only once Chun Ri had leaned in close did she announce: "The First Young Master Bai — you know him? He and Zhao Hongzhu have gotten involved!"

The expectant look on Chun Ri's face froze slowly in place.

Those words sounded oddly familiar. Like something that had left her own mouth just that morning.

Qiuyue pressed on, gesturing as she spoke: "And on top of that — Madam Bai went personally to the Qin estate to arrange the marriage! Guess what happened next?"

Chun Ri pressed her lips together, stepped back to the chopping board, and resumed chopping.

She could not believe she had sat there listening to Qiuyue's nonsense. What could Qiuyue possibly know?

Seeing Chun Ri stop responding, Qiuyue grew frantic — she had a belly full of tremendous secrets and no audience, and simply could not hold it in! If Chun Ri wouldn't ask, she'd circle around behind her and pester: "Guess! Come on, guess!"

Chun Ri's cleaver hit the board in a steady rhythm, the pork belly being reduced to neat square pieces. She kept chopping and said with deliberate boredom: "I can't guess."

Qiuyue couldn't hold back any longer: "The Old Madam was nearly worked to death!"

"How surprising," Chun Ri said flatly, but inwardly she was quietly marveling at the mistress's foresight.

A rumor that had gone out from her own mouth just this very morning, and by evening — the sun barely set — was already coming back through Qiuyue's lips. The rumor had clearly spread through every street and alley in the city.

Qiuyue only knew how to watch the excitement from the sidelines. She had heard a rumor and come home to repeat it, with no awareness whatsoever of what kind of enormous wave those few sentences would send crashing through the capital.

Zhao Hongzhu's reputation was ruined from this day forward. She was already the daughter of a convicted traitor who had returned from exile — the great houses of the capital regarded her with no small suspicion, waiting to see how she would conduct herself. Now she had first become entangled in an ambiguous affair with Qin Shanyue, a married man, and then gotten mixed up with Bai Yunhe as well. How was that behavior any different from a woman of the pleasure quarters?

The relationship between the Bai and Qin families was finished for good. They had become the laughingstock of the entire capital. Both were households of standing and consequence; going forward in the capital, they would never be able to fully shake each other off. Like two strips of dog-skin plaster stuck together — at the sight of each other, they would be irritated, yet would remain adhesively, inextricably joined, impossible to peel apart.

Qin Shanyue was one thing — he had stubbornly chosen to marry Zhao Hongzhu and had surely long since thought through these consequences. But Bai Yunhe had truly been struck by lightning out of a clear sky. He was just half a year away from marrying his superior's daughter. The Bai family's foundations were thin; Bai Yunhe had spent enormous effort making himself worthy in the eyes of the Minister of Justice — keeping no maidservant as a concubine, even swearing never to take a second wife in his life, which had delighted the Minister and prompted him to pave the way for a smooth and promising career path. A bright future had been right within his grasp — and now this had appeared, throwing the Bai household into an uproar as well.

Words, too, can kill.

"Chun Ri, are you even listening to me?" Qiuyue had just gotten to the part about Zhao Hongzhu possibly being a reincarnated fox spirit when she looked up and found Chun Ri lost in thought over her chopping, apparently far more interested in the meat on the board than in anything Qiuyue had to say. She stamped her foot in indignation, cried "I'm ignoring you!" and made to run out — then was called back by Chun Ri to pick the vegetables.

"No vegetable picking, no dinner tonight!"

The two maidservants bickered and chattered, the small kitchen warm and smoky with the ordinary pleasures of the evening. In the study of Fog Forest Courtyard, an oil lamp was lit. An autumn breeze stirred the air. The sun hung distantly behind a tall mountain, sinking lazily downward, its orange light painting the horizon into a sweep of evening color. The rivers lay gentle, and the world was soft and warm.

chapters.title: Chapter 31
chapters.content:
The man had apparently never been so humiliated in his life. Even as he walked, his brow remained locked in a deep furrow. When he spoke again, his voice had dropped two registers lower than before, coming out thick and muffled: "The specifics must be conveyed by the Master himself — this subordinate does not dare to pass on anything that might be mistaken. If you can manage it, come to meet the Master tomorrow."

At the mention of "the Master," a look of genuine admiration passed across the man's face, and his tone became more solemn: "The Master is very eager to see you."

Shen Shizhuo had no particular warmth toward this unknown Master, nor much desire to meet him. But things had reached this point, and he had no other path to follow. He would have to see it through.

"What is your name?"

"This subordinate is called Zhuifeng."

"Understood. Tomorrow at noon I will go out for a while — have him name a location." He added: "And the people in my courtyard—"

"Young Master, please have no worry on that account." Zhuifeng was quick to fill in the rest: "This subordinate will stand watch day and night. Not a single intruder will slip through."

Shen Shizhuo felt reassured. He gave Zhuifeng a lift of the chin — a dismissal — and Zhuifeng clasped his hands together and withdrew.

Zhuifeng took the kitchen path on his way out; one flip over the kitchen wall led directly out of the courtyard without having to pass through the forest. Passing the kitchen, he could see through the window the silhouette of Qiuyue stirring something at the stove.

His expression cooled by three degrees. He kept his face stiff and moved to scale the wall, making no effort to acknowledge Qiuyue — but Qiuyue had already spotted him. She muttered at him with visible displeasure: "Trading on looks and getting nowhere. What a disgrace."

She thought she was speaking quietly. But a man trained in martial arts has sharp ears, and Zhuifeng caught even the faint sound of her snort with perfect clarity. Incensed, he stamped the ground hard and vaulted over the wall.

By the time Zhuifeng left Fog Forest Courtyard, it was the deep of the night. He had not ridden a horse; relying entirely on his lightness skills, he flew along the ridgelines and eaves of rooftops. The city gates between inner and outer city had already been locked for the night, and with tensions running high, he could not afford to flash a pass and draw attention at the gates — so he timed it carefully and waited at the gatehouse for the hour of opening.

As he waited, Zhuifeng felt a warmth slowly kindling in his chest.

The Young Master had agreed to meet the Master. Whatever else happened, this was good news.

By then it was nearly dawn. A pale bluish light had begun to seep across the horizon. The moment the gates swung open, Zhuifeng swept in like a wind and made straight for Qilin Street.

* * *

The early morning of late autumn was not yet cold — the sun's light was mild enough to look at directly. Birds hopped lightly over the red-brick, green-tiled rooftops, and thick white clouds pressed down from above; glance upward, and you could see them blazing gold at the edges.

Today was fine weather. But it was not a good day.

Not for the Qin household, at any rate — because yesterday, their General Qin Shanyue had petitioned the Emperor for an imperial marriage decree.

An imperial decree of marriage was an honor ordinarily reserved for ministers of the second rank and above. It should have been cause for rejoicing. But the one he had petitioned for was the person living in Burnt Book Court.

By now, Zhao Hongzhu's name could not even be spoken aloud in the Qin estate. Since the Old Madam had collapsed in fury, been revived with the ginseng decoction, and come back to herself, she had developed a hatred for Zhao Hongzhu that went down to the bone. She would have liked nothing better than to drag her out and have her chopped to pieces. She raged constantly, threatening to have Zhao Hongzhu dragged out and drowned in a pig cage — but Zhao Hongzhu was installed in Burnt Book Court under the protection of guards who had no loyalties but to Qin Shanyue himself. The Old Madam could not get through the door.

Every servant and stablehand in the Qin estate combined was no match for those soldiers at the gate.

The Old Madam carried a fire in her chest that threatened to make her combust. Anything that displeased her eyes brought on a tirade of cursing. The maidservants and servant women attending her in Rosy Sunset Garden had all been punished lately. Twice the Old Madam had become so disoriented that she mistook Qin Shanyue for his long-dead father, clung to him, and wept and raged until she had exhausted herself into unconsciousness — but her sleep was never long. After only an hour or two she would startle awake again and begin her frantic howling anew.

The maidservants of the Qin estate were visibly wasting away.

Yet none of it could stop Qin Shanyue and Zhao Hongzhu's wedding.

* * *

At daybreak, as the first threads of morning light fell on Burnt Book Court, Zhao Hongzhu was already awake.

The Qin estate had been in turmoil these past days. Qin Shanyue had repeatedly tried to send her away to the small courtyard he had prepared for her outside the estate, but she had refused.

The harder things became, the less she was willing to leave. It was simply her nature — a contrary stubbornness baked into her bones. When others found her presence unbearable, she made a point of appearing before them in full bloom. When others came at her with trouble, she returned it tenfold, until they trembled at the sight of her. The Qin Old Madam was no exception.

She intended to be like a nail driven straight into the Old Madam's eye.

Qin Shanyue understood her nature well enough to stop pressing. These days he was busy regardless — he was gone from the moment daylight broke. When Zhao Hongzhu stepped out of the bedroom, a soldier told her matter-of-factly: "General Qin has already left."

Gone again.

Zhao Hongzhu felt a faint hollowness stir inside her.

She was not a woman who needed to lean on a man. But recent days had been relentless, and she could not stop herself from wanting some comfort. With Qin Shanyue absent, she went into his study and browsed through his books.

Qin Shanyue had never much cared for books; the ones in his study were piled without any order. Some were memorials he had drafted himself; others were personal letters to and from various correspondents. No matter how confidential the content, they were all stacked carelessly on the desk. Zhao Hongzhu went through them one by one, and gradually the restlessness inside her settled.

This was the place where Qin Shanyue kept his most sensitive secrets, and she knew it. Every letter here, if taken outside, could potentially ruin him irreparably. Yet she moved through it freely, and the soldiers outside treated her with the same deference they gave Qin Shanyue himself.

Whatever state she was reduced to, Qin Shanyue always loved her. As long as she had Qin Shanyue, she feared nothing.

Zhao Hongzhu studied those letters, quietly counting the days in her head.

Two days ago, Qin Shanyue had petitioned on her behalf. The Emperor had set the wedding date for half a month away.

An imperial decree wedding was not normally rushed like this — three to five months of preparation was standard. But she had a second matter to attend to after marrying Qin Shanyue: the rehabilitation of her father's name.

Years ago, the entire Zhao household had been framed for treason, with Prince Duan as the mastermind behind it all. Qin Shanyue had told her that the Emperor was planning to act against Prince Duan during the autumn imperial hunt, uncover the evidence from back then, and clear the Zhao family's name. For that reason, her wedding had to be completed before the hunt.

A wedding was the most important event of a woman's life, but for Zhao Hongzhu, the honor and the lives of every soul in the Zhao household mattered more. So she felt no grief over the haste of the occasion.

Moreover, an imperial-decree wedding, however rushed, would be no less grand for it. That very morning, several groups of seamstresses had already arrived. The wedding robes being prepared were encrusted with pearls and precious stones in quantities none of the seamstresses had ever seen before; Zhao Hongzhu thought, with some amusement, that by the time all of that was sewn into the fabric, she might actually be crushed under the weight of it.

More precious than any of it was a single coral bead.

It had been ground from South Sea red coral — a deep, vivid red. Qin Shanyue had polished it himself, not recently, but years ago, shortly after they had been betrothed. He had taken a blade, found the right angle, and cut it from the coral, then day after day, painstakingly ground it down on a whetstone with his own hands.

He had never had the chance to give it to her before they were separated. Many years later, he had unearthed it again from storage. That red bead was a perfect match to her name: Hongzhu — Red Bead.

The red bead was to be set into her wedding headdress and bridal robes. This was Zhao Hongzhu's own request. She wanted to carry Qin Shanyue's love from when he was eighteen years old with her all the way to the very end of her days.

As she thought of all this, a small smile touched her face.

Round and round, through everything — it had always come back to her.

While she was lost in thought, someone knocked at the study door.

"Miss Zhao."

The soldier outside had softened his voice, but it still came out rough and low: "Your newly purchased maidservants have arrived."

Zhao Hongzhu returned to herself and rose to open the door.

Outside the study stood a soldier with clasped fists, and behind him four young maidservants who looked to be around fifteen or sixteen — all bright-eyed and quick-looking, dressed in pink skirts, their hair done in two neat circles on either side of their heads. They bowed to her in unison, voices ringing out together: "Greetings to the Mistress."

Ever since Lancao was gone, Zhao Hongzhu had had no one to attend to her. Qin Shanyue had initially thought to assign her a few capable maidservants from within the Qin estate, but those women were all jittery and unsettled with the recent chaos — even if transferred to Zhao Hongzhu's side, they wouldn't serve her with any real devotion. It had seemed better to simply purchase some maidservants from outside, ones with clean backgrounds who knew nothing of what was happening, and give them to Zhao Hongzhu to cultivate as her own trusted attendants.

Zhao Hongzhu looked each of them over in turn, asked their names, assigned them new ones, gave a brief outline of their daily duties, and returned to the study.

The grief that Lancao's death had left behind grew heavier rather than lighter with each passing day. She had no heart to accept other maidservants yet — their faces only reminded her of what she had lost. So she simply sat at Qin Shanyue's writing desk in a daze, and when exhaustion crept over her, she folded her arms on his paper and slept.

That was what Qin Shanyue found when he pushed open the study door and stepped inside.

A girl with striking, richly drawn features, asleep at his desk. At some point a brushstroke had left a mark across her cheek. The quiet, sleeping image of her overlapped with the memory of years ago, when they would study together at the same table. Qin Shanyue should have felt warmth rise in his chest at the sight — but without knowing why, the image of Bai Qingli suddenly surfaced in his mind: sitting at this same desk, sorting through his correspondence for him.

Qin Shanyue's heart sank.

He could not explain it himself. For days now, that strange dream had been coiling through his thoughts and refusing to leave. He kept returning, over and over, to Bai Qingli's despair and anguish as he had lived it from inside the dream.

"You're back?"

At that moment, Zhao Hongzhu stirred awake, rubbing her eyes, and smiled at Qin Shanyue.

Qin Shanyue forcibly dug Bai Qingli out of his mind and nodded back with a small smile.

He was back. He had come back to Zhao Hongzhu's side. He absolutely could not allow himself to think about Bai Qingli any further. Everything between them had been destroyed by Bai Qingli's own hands. She did not deserve his love. Even if she came back to him in tears, begging, he would not soften.

"Back now," Qin Shanyue murmured, and then heard Zhao Hongzhu ask: "How are things coming along with my father's case?"

Given that the matter involved a charge of treason, the details were highly confidential — but Zhao Hongzhu was the last surviving member of the Zhao family, and she had always been sharp and perceptive. Qin Shanyue had never kept secrets from her. He told her directly whatever he knew; now, at her question, he answered honestly.

"All the evidence has been secured. We are only waiting for the right moment." Qin Shanyue smoothed her hair gently, his voice unusually tender: "We marry first. After the rehabilitation, I will take you to pay our respects at your father's grave. Have no worry — I will personally see Prince Duan brought to justice."

In the afternoon stillness of the study, the General's voice was steady and calm, his expression soft. Every word he spoke carried the weight of iron resolve and painted a vision of a better future. Zhao Hongzhu nestled her head against his palm, her eyes full of trust.

* * *

In the quiet of the afternoon, Shen Shizhuo also used the pretext of a nap to shut his bedroom door, then slipped out through the window, scaled the outer wall, and mounted the fast horse Zhuifeng had ready for him. Together, the two of them rode into the city.

In the daytime, the gates between inner and outer city were open. The outer city was a place of earthen houses and brick walls, where people in rough-woven clothes carried shoulderpoles to sell their goods along the road. The road itself was yellow dirt. But once inside the inner city, the ground changed to neatly fitted grey granite slabs, the gaps between them clean and even. The people who passed were well-spoken, and there were noticeably more richly dressed figures and fine carriages. No street vendors here — only two rows of storefronts, all with their doors wide open, bustling with customers.

Zhuifeng led Shen Shizhuo to an unmarked residence that had the look of a prosperous merchant's home. Stepping inside revealed a winding covered walkway, pavilions and water features, and a working stone fountain made from a diverted stream. A palanquin was waiting by the entrance. The moment Shen Shizhuo stepped inside, Zhuifeng fell back a few paces, and the four men bearing the palanquin knelt and waited for him to mount it.

Shen Shizhuo had no taste for such displays. He didn't move — he simply lifted his eyes and gave Zhuifeng a cold look.

Zhuifeng registered the mood at once and immediately waved them off. The four men carried the empty palanquin away, and Zhuifeng led Shen Shizhuo inside on foot, explaining as they walked: "The estate is very large and the Master's study is at some distance. We didn't want the Young Master to tire himself."

Large was no exaggeration. From the entrance to the study, two trained martial artists walked for a full half-hour. Along the way, every structure was elaborate, every surface rich and ornamented.

Shen Shizhuo was already forming impressions of this unknown Master he had never met. This was more than wealth — this was power of a kind that money alone could not buy. This location, this ostentation, was not available at any price.

The estate appeared deserted. Perhaps knowing Shen Shizhuo would come today, the grounds had been deliberately cleared — not a single maidservant was visible the entire walk. They went straight to the study door, where Zhuifeng stopped, faced the study, and bowed: "Master, the Young Master has arrived."

Not a sound came from inside. Zhuifeng waited three quiet breaths, then stepped aside, clasped his hands toward Shen Shizhuo, and said: "Young Master, please go in."

Shen Shizhuo looked at the study's wooden door. It was a deep vermilion, carved with an intricately patterned flower that announced itself as valuable at a glance. Midday sunlight filtered through it, casting a dark grey shadow on the floor.

Shen Shizhuo stared at the shadow of the flower and thought of the years he had lived in the old temple.

The doors in the temple had been like this too — but instead of carved flowers, they had only plain crossbeam frames. When the light came through, it left a clean, square impression on the floor. When he had been bored enough, he would hop across those squares of light.

He thought: during those years when he was still growing, scrambling through the mountain forests like a wild dog in the woods — while this Master lived here in this bronze-tiled, gilded place, did he ever spare a single day's thought for him? Did he ever look?

Tangled, turbulent thoughts flooded his mind, but in the midst of them he found himself strangely calm. He had come this far; there was no retreating now. He reached out, pushed the door open with ease, and stepped through.

Inside was a large study — spacious and bright. The first thing that met his eyes were several rows of shelves lined with books and scrolls. To the right stood a large writing desk with inkstone, brush, paper and ink. On the left wall hung a painting.

The painting was of a strikingly beautiful woman in a pomegranate-red skirt. Her features were nearly identical to Shen Shizhuo's own — and yet though the resemblance was there, her eyes carried a living, luminous allure, a natural and innate seductiveness that no man could ever possess. Such beauty needed nothing but that face to overturn the world; Shen Shizhuo could well imagine the devastation she must have wrought in life.

The window on the left side was open. The midday sun blazed in, illuminating every suspended mote of dust in the air. A light breeze passed through, and the woman in the painting seemed, for a moment, to come alive.

From the moment Shen Shizhuo's gaze fell on the painting, something surged up from deep within him — a strange, powerful feeling, as though someone had seized his heart in a fist. He could not breathe. The blood throughout his body seemed to rush upward and then plunge downward in the space of a heartbeat. His hands and feet went cold; his heart hammered.

It was a feeling unlike anything he had ever experienced before. For a moment he had no idea how to compose himself, and simply stood there, transfixed by the painting.

"That is your mother."

A deep, steady voice came from behind him. Shen Shizhuo turned sharply — and found a tall, upright figure standing at his back.

The man had a broad, square face. He wore a deep slate-blue robe richly embroidered all over with four-clawed dragons in gold thread, and at his left hip hung a black-lacquered blade. Though no longer young, his back was ramrod straight, and around him hung the air of someone tempered by decades of battle. When Shen Shizhuo turned, the man was looking at him with a smile.

It was a smile distilled from time — from having lived through storms and watched the world change, and let it all settle into something quiet at the bottom.

"This is the first time we have met," the man said, "but I have thought of you countless times. My name is Ji Chang'an. The world outside calls me Prince Duan."

* * *

chapters.title: Chapter 32
chapters.content:
The title "Prince Duan" landed on Shen Shizhuo like a blow, jolting him fully alert.

He had lived in the mountains for years, but he knew the weight those three words carried: imperial blood, the highest lineage of royalty — the kind of man that every commoner on the street had to kneel and crane their neck upward just to see. With a single wave of his hand, he could send a great wave crashing across the land.

That was what power looked like.

"Prince Duan." Shen Shizhuo let the syllables rest on his tongue, his voice carrying neither pleasure nor displeasure — as calm as if he felt no weight at all beneath the name, no sense of wealth or royal authority.

Or perhaps he felt it — but simply didn't care.

Whatever Prince Duan might be to the world, it had nothing to do with him. What he had ever wanted was never this. He wanted a Fog Forest Courtyard, one person, two noisy maidservants, a strip of moonlight, a cup of wine on the table, a stray lock of hair on the pillow. That was enough.

As Shen Shizhuo studied Prince Duan, Prince Duan studied him in turn.

Shen Shizhuo had his mother's face — a work of almost supernatural beauty — but he was, after all, a man: his frame was larger, his features angular and strong, with less of that captivating softness and more of a cool and remote austerity. He stood quietly in place, and Prince Duan glanced from his face to the face in the painting on the wall, and felt the years spin past him.

"I hear from Zhuifeng that you carry the surname Shen. You must have taken your mother's family name." Prince Duan spoke again. He seemed in no hurry to pour out his years of longing, nor did he reach for the subject of blood ties. He simply spoke of Shen Shizhuo's mother.

"Your mother's name was Ruyan — Shen Ruyan. She came from an ordinary background, born to a merchant family. But she was adored and indulged at home. The first time I traveled south of the Yangtze, I spotted your mother on a boat."

"The skies south of the river are a deep blue, and the waters a brilliant green. Your mother was dressed in a scholar's robe of pure white — disguised as a man, going out to explore. That was how I came to know her. We traveled the mountains and rivers together. One day she drank too much and asked if I had a wife. I said I did not. She let her hair down and told me she was a woman. She asked whether I would be willing to marry her."

"She did not know I was Prince Duan. Had she known, she would never have asked."

The misty rains of the south of the Yangtze are soft on the heart, and even the wind there is warm and gentle — gentle enough not to startle the butterfly in a beauty's hair. A girl born in the flowers did not know the cruelties of the capital. With nothing but courage and love, she ignored her parents' objections and followed her beloved to the city.

The capital. What was the capital? Elegance and splendor on the surface, debauchery and license underneath — a book written in the language of virtue and righteousness, its pages soaked in human desire. A beauty from south of the river stepped in, and could never find her way back out. The further in she went, the muddier the story became. Two people who had once stood in the clouds both fell, slowly, to earth. By the time they looked at each other again, they could barely remember what love had looked like at the beginning.

"After your mother followed me to the capital, she did have some comfortable days. I knew she was lively by nature and hated to be caged, so I never restrained her. I gave her a few maidservants, let her wander the streets freely on horseback. But she was too beautiful, Shizhuo — you should understand this. Sometimes it is not a matter of having a good heart, or being innocent. Innocence offers no immunity from misfortune. All that matters is that you have something others covet. So long as she had it, someone would inevitably try to take it."

What followed involved secrets of the imperial household — intimate, ugly matters — but Prince Duan spoke of it without the slightest evasion, with a directness that bordered on brutality.

"Your mother accompanied me on a visit to the palace. I went before the Empress Dowager to petition for permission to marry her. I said I wanted to give her everything — I wanted to name her my Princess Consort, I wanted to spend my life with her, one wife, one man, for eternity. My mother refused. In her eyes, this woman who had sailed out from south of the river was a water snake that had coiled herself around her son and bewitched him. She deliberately made things difficult for your mother — using the pretext of teaching her court etiquette, she kept her in the palace. At the time I thought: let my mother spend time with her and perhaps she would come to accept her. So I did not interfere."

"Then something happened."

Prince Duan's long lashes dropped over his eyes. He paused, like someone bearing the slow fall of a lash, then quietly continued: "My elder brother — the Emperor, a man who possessed every beauty the world had to offer — had never encountered a woman like your mother. Simple, kind, even a little foolish, but lovely in a way he had no words for. A piece of summer ice and cool wind. A moonlit beauty he had never seen before, a shadow from south of the river. He fell in love with your mother in a way he could not control."

"Perhaps he hesitated, perhaps he wavered — but in the end, he chose to make your mother his. Afterward, the reason he gave was that he had been drunk and mistaken her for one of his consorts. He was the Emperor: there were only two fates for any woman he had touched. Enter the palace as a consort, or hang herself. The matter caused a stir in the palace for a time. My mother could restrain her own son, but she could not restrain an Emperor. In the end, your mother was given the title of Noble Consort Li."

Noble Consort Li.

Even those two characters alone could conjure the image of that bewitching face.

"And then?" Prince Duan had been silent for a long moment. Shen Shizhuo finally spoke.

He could guess at some of it — the story that followed could not have been good. But he needed to hear it to the end.

He needed to know what had happened on this earth in the years before he was born. He needed to know: in what form did he come into this world? And in those years when he was young and unknowing, how had the people around him seen him?

"I could not accept it." Prince Duan stood at a distance, still in that posture — one hand resting on the blade, eyes moving between Shen Shizhuo and the painting — and with a voice of absolute, settled calm, he repeated, deliberately: "I. Could. Not. Accept. It."

No man could have endured such a humiliation. From the night his woman was taken from him, he understood many things clearly.

Such as why — why everyone wanted that throne.

Because the one who sat at the very top was the law itself.

"Afterward—" Prince Duan paused, then said quietly: "You are not a woman. You cannot understand the humiliation of having something taken from you in that way. If my imperial brother had been a good man, perhaps it would have been different. But he was not. My brother was born with everything, and so he never learned to treasure anything. When he was happy, he placed her on a pedestal. He felled a thousand-year-old tree from the northern mountains and had it carved into a bed for her, because she admired that kind of wood. She missed the south of the river, so he transplanted all the flowers and trees from the south to the capital, building her a miniature Jiangnan inside the palace walls. But when he was displeased, he would throw scalding soup on her, have her kneel and crawl across the floor, force her to slap herself across the face in front of all the palace women. Two months of that, and she no longer wanted to live. The night I went to find her, she came to me, and we were together."

It was a sordid history by any measure — and yet when Prince Duan spoke of it, his eyes were full of warmth and tenderness: "Those were the best six months of our lives. But that kind of happiness couldn't last. The palace was full of eyes. Our secret was exposed before long. The Emperor could not bring himself to kill her, and could not kill me — so the only thing he could do was separate us. I was sent to the frontier, where I have remained, year after year, for decades. Wind and frost and open skies, and twice I nearly died out there — once on the brink of being buried at the border, once nearly cut down by a short blade. But I clung to that last breath and survived."

"I could not die. I was still dreaming of returning to the capital and seeing your mother again. But I learned much later — half a month after I left, your mother was found to be with child. The Emperor wanted to keep the child. Your mother did not. She tried to take her own life several times. Once a person has no will to live, they lose all fear. She came close to dying on one of those attempts, and that finally frightened the Emperor. In the end, the Empress Dowager stepped in — your mother was sent to the Imperial Clan Court to recuperate and quietly bring the child to term."

Prince Duan's voice grew slightly colder: "After your mother gave birth to you, the Emperor briefly considered naming you Crown Prince. That crossed a line for the Empress Dowager. That same night, your mother was sent off with a bowl of poison. Only you were left. The Empress Dowager's people took you away, and neither the Emperor nor I could find you for years. The Empress Dowager's account to both of us was that you had gone with your mother. But neither the Emperor nor I believed her. Heirs in the imperial household were scarce — at the time the Emperor didn't have a single son, and I had no children and was unmarried. We didn't know whether you were the Emperor's child or mine — but you were the only imperial prince in the entire Da Feng royal family. However much the Empress Dowager despised your mother, she would never harm an imperial prince."

"It was only in recent years, as the Empress Dowager aged and grew close to the end, that we picked up a trace of wind. But by the time our people reached the mountain, the old temple had been slaughtered, and you had vanished."

"I still don't know who did it. It could have been anyone. Even the Empress Dowager herself, perhaps — the Emperor now has an imperial prince, born of the Empress, a legitimate heir of the main line. Eliminating you to protect the Crown Prince's position would have been entirely rational. It might also have been the Crown Prince's maternal family — the current Empress and your mother were once bitter rivals at court. Your mother, in self-defense, once moved against her; if the Empress learned of your existence, striking against you would have been natural. Fortunately, you did not die."

All the bitterness and hardship and love and hatred of the past were glossed over in a few sparse sentences. Prince Duan finished, making no attempt to gauge Shen Shizhuo's reactions, and simply heaped all of it onto him, letting him process it himself.

"You are grown now. The Empress Dowager may not be fond of you, but you are still of imperial blood. I trust she would not have withheld your upbringing. These things I believe you can think through yourself. I will tell you only one thing: your identity was given to you at birth — it is not something you can choose. If you do not compete, do not fight, you will be competed for and fought over, just as your mother was. You will carry regret to your grave as I have."

"Furthermore — not only have I found you, but the Emperor's people have also traced your trail. They have not yet traced it to you directly, but once he finds you, he will be certain to acknowledge you and bring you into the palace. At that point, you will have no choice in the matter."

When Prince Duan reached that last line, he seemed to have exhausted himself completely. He waved a weary hand, dismissing Shen Shizhuo to find his own way out.

Shen Shizhuo walked out on his own.

As he stepped over the threshold, he turned his head back, just briefly.

Prince Duan had already moved to stand before the painting. Through the window, Shen Shizhuo could see him reaching out to trace the face of the woman on the wall with a gentle hand, smiling.

A canvas of red dust, half a lifetime of tears.

Shen Shizhuo paused for a moment, then turned and walked away.

He passed out of that beautiful, extravagant courtyard and stepped back into the bustle of the capital. The sounds of people and the noise of the city gradually filtered into his ears, and the tension he had carried inside the estate slowly drained away. He rode in silence for a while, then mounted his horse and left.

Ten thousand riches and a thousand splendors — to him, nothing but clouds passing before the eye. He had no interest in the blood ties he had just been told of, and he had no intention of walking the path Prince Duan had laid out for him.

He wanted none of this boundless wealth. He had no desire to meddle in those buried old affairs. He only wanted to find a quiet, out-of-the-way place, hold a handful of moonlight in his palms, and walk through whatever years remained in peace.

He needed to move Bai Qingli first — find a new place to live, shake off those watchful eyes, make preparations, and leave ahead of time.

But Prince Duan's reach was long. He would need to plan with care.

* * *

These thoughts swept through Shen Shizhuo's mind, were settled, and were set aside. He returned to Fog Forest Courtyard in the afternoon, slipped back through the window, rolled around on the bed for a few moments to appear freshly woken, then got up and went to find Bai Qingli.

When he found her, Bai Qingli was talking with Qiuyue and Chun Ri. All three of them had settled on going to see the lantern festival that evening.

The Da Feng dynasty had been founded through military victory. In the early years of the dynasty, the final triumph had come in the tenth month, and the troops had returned at night, welcomed by households who lit their lanterns and crowded the city gates to greet them — a scene of magnificent celebration, with all the people of the nation pouring out to receive them.

After that, every year when a new Emperor was enthroned or when the Emperor returned from ancestral rites, the occasion was fixed to this same date.

So Da Feng had this custom: on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth of the tenth month each year, there were lantern festivals in the evening. All women — whether unmarried daughters from great households or married women — were permitted to walk freely. The city gates between inner and outer city were left open all night, and the crowds were allowed to make merry and enjoy the prosperous age together.

They had another half month before their new identity tablets would be ready, and they couldn't stay in the capital much longer — why not go out and see it one last time?

Qiuyue adored the lantern festival above all things. There would be people everywhere, all manner of delicious food, riddle games on the lanterns, street performers putting on shows — and, of course, people throwing embroidered balls.

At every lantern festival, young men and women of eligible age would come out to enjoy the evening. If someone caught sight of a person they fancied, they would toss an embroidered ball toward them. If the other person caught it, it was taken as a heaven-ordained match.

The balls came in all kinds: balls the size of a head made from silk ribbon, balls no larger than a baby's fist woven from rattan, or balls carved or braided by hand — ivory balls for the wealthy, golden balls, or plain ones made from grass reeds. All were welcome. Qiuyue had plucked some branches from the fog trees around the courtyard, carefully clipped and bent them into shape, then threaded needle and thread through the middle and stitched them into a ball. She had tucked a small bell inside, so that every time the ball was tossed, the bell inside went jingle-jingle.

This was her embroidered ball. Her precious embroidered ball. It was going to find her the devoted, devoted man of her dreams.

When Shen Shizhuo came around to the window of the bedroom and looked inside, he saw Bai Qingli sitting upright in a chair, holding a cup fashioned from bamboo, watching with quiet amusement as Qiuyue and Chun Ri chattered and showed off their respective embroidered balls. The water in her cup had just been brought to a boil and was still releasing curls of steam; the delicate, rolling mist softened the lines of Bai Qingli's eyes and brows, and she pressed her lips together in a small smile. All the tangled worries in Shen Shizhuo's chest dissolved at once.

The lantern festival... was apparently also a good place for a rendezvous.

After the festival, he would talk to Bai Qingli about all that complicated mess. For now, he only wanted to watch her smile a little longer.

* * *

That evening, Shen Shizhuo drove the carriage and brought all three women into the city.

Bai Qingli, Qiuyue, and Chun Ri all changed into plain, unremarkable clothes. Bai Qingli also wore a wide-brimmed hat with a gauze veil to keep from being recognized. The four of them found a wine shop, left the carriage there, and then set out on foot along the outer city streets.

The road was lined with every kind of lantern, and vendors hawked their wares in every direction. A small lantern to carry in the hand cost around fifteen copper coins; a sky lantern for making wishes cost fifty; floating river lanterns were the cheapest at five coins each.

When they climbed down from the carriage, Chun Ri and Qiuyue both jumped down on their own. When it came time for Bai Qingli to descend, Shen Shizhuo stepped forward to help her down.

Once on the ground, the street unfolded before them — a long avenue lit by shifting, flickering candlelight from end to end. The crowd surged and jostled, and in the distance came a sharp crack and a roar of voices.

Bai Qingli raised her eyes.

Fireworks.

Dazzling as a shower of meteors, more brilliant than the Milky Way. A child sat on its father's shoulders clapping and shouting. An unmarried girl stole a shy glance toward the person she loved. The lanterns were just being lit, and the night was at its finest.

Qiuyue had already grabbed Chun Ri and bolted toward the excitement. She wanted to see the action; Chun Ri knew perfectly well that the mistress and Shen Shizhuo would want to walk together, and didn't want to be in the way.

In moments, both maidservants had disappeared into the crowd. Shen Shizhuo stood at Bai Qingli's side, shielding her from the press of people, and guided her forward along the street.

Bai Qingli had never experienced anything like this before. The Bai household had strict rules: when she was unmarried, she was confined to the estate every day. On the rare occasion she had seen the lantern festival, it was from inside a palanquin, from a careful distance — never out in the crowd. After marrying into the Qin household, she had been careful and guarded at every turn. In two lifetimes, this was the first time.

Candlelight glimmered, figures moved like shadows, and she slowed her steps, drinking in the fullness of the living world.

It was good to be alive.

She was watching the world; Shen Shizhuo was watching her. As the two of them strolled along the street, a street vendor sidled up with a grin: "Young master, aren't you going to buy a lantern for your lady? Very auspicious for wishes!"

Bai Qingli had barely reacted, but Shen Shizhuo's face had already gone vivid red. He said nothing — only flicked a glance at Bai Qingli and murmured, "We're just passing through, we're not making any wishes" — but his hand had already honestly counted out fifty copper coins and placed them in the vendor's palm.

The vendor handed them a slip of paper and told them to write whatever they wished. Shen Shizhuo didn't dare look at Bai Qingli's face, terrified she would see through his embarrassment. It was just being called "lady" — why should he mind? They had already exchanged their vows. She was, by all rights, his lady.

Shen Shizhuo's face went even redder — brighter than the fireworks overhead — and he could not stop himself from glancing back at Bai Qingli again.

Bai Qingli wasn't looking at him. She took the paper and brush and stood there thinking about what to write.

At that moment, the two of them stood at the edge of the street — the young man clear and unworldly, the young woman like a breeze through the trees. Perhaps it was the particular gentleness of his gaze, but even the candle flames around them seemed to burn a little brighter. The firelight fell across both their faces, and Shen Shizhuo's heart quickened again, without his permission.

After Bai Qingli finished writing and placed the slip inside the lantern, Shen Shizhuo lit it, then watched it rise — the way a man watches his love beginning to ascend — as the lantern floated upward, drifted into the night, and mingled with all the others until he could no longer tell which one was his.

They walked a little further along the street, and in the distance they spotted a lantern riddle station.

It had been set up on a wide open patch in the middle of the avenue — a tall wooden frame with many lanterns hanging from it, each bearing a written riddle. Solve one, win a prize. The prizes were mostly fine jewelry, each displayed in its own small wooden box, shimmering and sparkling under the lantern light.

Shen Shizhuo's eye went immediately to a long hairpin carved in the shape of a white lotus. He felt at once that Bai Qingli would like it. He couldn't help glancing over at her — and found she was already looking at it. Their eyes met for an instant. Without a word being spoken, he stepped forward to try for it.

Bai Qingli turned her head away for just a moment — and there was Shen Shizhuo already up at the front. In that brief exchange of glances, neither of them had said a word, but Bai Qingli understood immediately: he had gone to win that hairpin for her.

It was a strange feeling — as though her thoughts were being caught and understood by someone else with effortless ease. And yet she didn't feel like she was being watched or intruded upon. Perhaps because she trusted this person completely, bone-deep certain that Shen Shizhuo would never harm her, certain that whatever Shen Shizhuo did, it would always be for her good.

It was why she so particularly enjoyed being around him. She felt at ease. The time she had spent in Fog Forest Courtyard since her rebirth had been the most peaceful stretch of her new life.

The wind lifted the gauze veil of Bai Qingli's hat, revealing half her face. She watched Shen Shizhuo's back in silence, the way one might watch something warm.

* * *

"General." At that moment, on the other side of the wooden riddle frame, Qin Shanyue — out for the festival in a black brocade robe — and the servant boy behind him stood among the crowd. Through the frame and the gaps between the lanterns, from a distance, a figure had caught the servant boy's eye.

That figure looked so familiar. When the breeze lifted the gauze veil, the servant boy's skin prickled all over.

"Is that not the Mistress? She is with a man."

* * *

chapters.title: Chapter 33
chapters.content:
On the other side of the wooden frame, Qin Shanyue stood in his black brocade robe, gazing at Zhao Hongzhu, who was not far away.

Zhao Hongzhu had brought two young maidservants with her and was watching a street performance. She had always loved loud and lively scenes, and disliked being followed too closely — so Qin Shanyue had simply trailed along at a respectful distance behind her.

His eyes had never left Zhao Hongzhu. She was wearing a brilliant red dress today, and the sight of her was like looking at a wintersweet in full bloom. No one suited red the way she did. The moment he saw her, he felt himself sinking into another time and could not pull his gaze away. So when Bai Qingli's name broke in on him, Qin Shanyue startled.
